contradictions.note: That paper argues price/vol time-series models fail on crypto versus cross-asset structure.

A systematic falsification of 14 OHLCV intraday momentum signal families on MNQ/MGC finds none pass validation; this paper's SPY rule is a different instrument and absence of held-out test makes it vulnerable to the same critique.
Raschke rejects MA derivatives as edge (p.4 I) while 3.12 defines a two-MA rule.
Interview pushes ATR/large-target/trail exit menu; that paper finds faster take-profit not better than simple MACD — both non-findings on exit rules.

Carr and Lopez de Prado derive exits by simulating an OU fit of prices; this paper derives the optimal risk-transfer shape analytically under a premium principle, with no simulation and no price process, so it does not support or reproduce their simulated optimal rule.
That paper finds stop-loss rules can rescue flat momentum in emerging Asian equities; this paper is about CB intervention, not exits — they do not test the same mechanism.
That paper's in-sample-optimised OU pairs thresholds report high in-sample Sharpe but the overfitting critique applies; OTR avoids the grid search that paper uses.
That paper finds O-U pairs Sharpe above 1.9 only from in-sample-optimised thresholds; this paper claims no backtest needed but gives no market out-of-sample evidence.
That paper argues a learned intraday reweighting improves realized-measure forecasts; this one finds simple linear models win for crypto quantiles.

That paper finds trailing stop losses rarely raise expected or risk-adjusted returns on simulated AR(1) and systematic books; this paper finds tighter trailing and faster take-profit improve Sharpe, but only in-sample on crypto agent-swarm trades.
Library COT/positioning study on four majors also questions whether positioning-based currency predictability survives; same major universe.
Finds the commodity-currency carry link state-dependent, not permanent, versus the survey's unconditional carry average.
That replication shrinks most anomaly high-minus-low returns; this paper similarly finds the headline association collapses to 0.023 once the criterion is moved to publication time.
The decay paper's finding that published anomalies lose Sharpe over time is a warning the current paper does not address (no post-publication test).
Conflicting philosophy: qlikeHAR improves forecasts by matching the evaluation loss, whereas this paper argues the loss-minimising forecast is not the economically best one.
1990s-vintage models fail against a driftless random walk; Bakker would attribute that to rho near one and short horizons, which the excerpt does not test.
That paper reports large positive carry payoffs and a Sharpe near twice the stock market's, i.e. a mean, whereas this one finds near-zero means and near-uniform regimes.
That paper reports carry-unwind responses conditioned on JGB curve states, implying regime dependence the random-walk conclusion denies.

Predictive OFI on L1 NBBO at 10-second bars claims cross-asset mean IC +0.0044, pooled t=3.26; this paper's structural ICs are of similar tiny magnitude but fail pooled FDR - different construction (NBBO vs bar proxy), different horizon, so the two together say the effect is at most marginal and con

Lustig-Roussanov-Verdelhan report 4.8% p.a. net of bid-ask on a 37-currency carry sort (Sharpe 0.54); this paper finds a clean negative after costs on four pairs — the difference is breadth (37 vs 4), data (futures vs MT5 bars) and cost model, not a refutation of the premium.

Peso-problem/carry paper claims carry Sharpe ~2x equities and uncorrelated with standard factors; this paper (four pairs, policy-rate, retail costs) finds all carry configs negative after costs — sample and breadth are the likely source.
Claims ML long-short gains persist even with bounds-based sorting on a US panel; the essay's stance is that such ML backtest gains are usually false discoveries unless tested independently.
Reports whole-universe ML 'significantly outperforms' the CAPM in walk-forward tests; per the essay, such repeated-test evidence is exactly what needs a held-out check before it is believed.

Gold Standard Pairs Trading finds distance and cointegration pairs fail to beat the benchmark on NYSE shares 1990-2020; this paper claims dominance over SPY on ETFs — different universe and ends 2009.
The 151 chapter defines a dollar-neutral swap-spread arbitrage as if the spread reverts; this paper argues the negative spread can persist as demand-driven, limiting that arbitrage.
3.20 describes combining hundreds of thousands of faint ML alphas into a mega-alpha via weights; this paper argues the combo layer is noisy and suboptimal and should be bypassed.
Nelson-Siegel random walk fails to beat random walk out of sample; this paper's curvature relation is a model, not a forecast edge.
The 151 protective-put entry defines the structure and its break-even/max-loss payoff without testing hedging efficacy; Israelov finds that structure ineffective versus divestment.
Learning/optimal-default model is a rational-expectations-style explanation of the sign that this paper argues against.

AQR Alternative Thinking 2025 finds 196 buy-the-dip parameterisations on the S&P 500 average a Sharpe 0.04 BELOW passive; Trinity's trend/buy-the-dip-adjacent overlays are presented as risk reducers, and neither tests the same rule, but AQR's null is a caution that such overlays do not add Sharpe.
That paper finds the basis sharply negative in 2007-2009 (IG -243bp, HY -560bp), the opposite sign to the +7.5bp median here, showing the equilibrium this paper documents broke in crisis.
That paper treats PMPU COT shocks as signed information for producer equity; this one says PMPU positions move with price and output-unrelated trading, so the shock is partly endogenous to price.
Hedging-pressure strategy treats hedger positioning as a clean supply/demand signal; this paper argues hedger positions are price-responsive and not purely hedge-driven.
The simple 10-month SMA trend rule on 5 ETFs is a transparent multi-year test; this paper's one-year parameter-fitted ES result is not comparable evidence for trend-following generally.

The distress-premium puzzle reports distressed firms' stocks underperform; Altman reports defaulted debt returning about at high-yield level with lower monthly vol, a debt-vs-equity distinction to keep explicit.

That paper reports S&P 500 and Treasury yields move in the same direction with equities leading yields; Ilmanen's mean-reversion-via-Fed-policy cycle story is a different driver for yield moves and does not rely on equity leadership.
That tutorial finds momentum in a constrained 50-stock portfolio weak; here momentum is one of the themes with the lowest variance ratio (median 1.0), i.e. the least 'streaky' factor.

Value and momentum premia in 8 markets including 10 currencies: consistent with this paper's claim that FX premia live in styles (carry/momentum) rather than static exposure, but shows premia the Two Sigma paper assigns 0.00 to FX at the factor level.
That tutorial uses VIX and put-call to tilt a value-minus-growth portfolio; Lis's review warns complex sentiment measures lack demonstrated out-of-sample advantage and vary by period and asset.
That paper finds in-sample ML predictability in US equities does not persist out of sample; this one reports no OOS evidence in the abstract.
That paper finds simple US equity signals do not persist out of sample; this one claims large economic gains without reported OOS protocol.
Long-memory vs short-memory term-structure models on US yields; different dynamic assumption to the regime-shift structure here — the two specifications disagree about what drives premia.
Same family of MA/TRB rules on Chinese indexes, corrected with SPA, finds nothing after costs; this paper's DFRD+/- finds short-term value on MSCI indices.
Long-sample S&P MA timing shows no out-of-sample edge; here technical rules survive but conditionally and with variable profitability.
5.14 defines CDS-basis carry as buy-bond/buy-CDS; 11.5 uses a short CDS as a hedge against a long tranche. The two are different, not directly comparable, but both untested.
That paper tests MA timing on 155 years of S&P and finds no stable out-of-sample edge; 8.1 asserts the rule improves FX without testing it.
That paper segments volatility regimes retrospectively (change-point + clustering); this one is causal and online, so it is the setting the desk can test without look-ahead

That paper finds the EWMA(0.94)-to-realised-vol scaling coefficient always below the RiskMetrics value across 47 futures; this paper treats EWMA as a benchmark rather than testing its scaling, but does not overturn or confirm that calibration finding.
Caveat rather than finding: the volatility proxy used here is a rolling SD of log returns, which is an imperfect proxy; that paper shows imperfect proxies can flip model-comparison rankings.

HAR-RV encodes long memory in realized vol; RFSV says the apparent long memory is an artefact of a rough (H~0.1) process read through long-memory estimators, though RFSV forecasts are only claimed to match, not beat, HAR.
Warns that forecast comparisons on imperfect volatility proxies and common loss functions can select the worse model.
Both aim at fast calibration but by different routes (closed-form characteristic function for Heston vs neural-network surrogate for rough models) — they compete for speed, not the same models.
HAR-RV gets long memory from deterministic additive daily/weekly/monthly RV components; this paper's SV is a stochastic AR(1) state — competing descriptions of the same persistence.

The QC skewness-based FX long/short is a directional rule on four pairs; this paper says the carry return is partly tail-risk compensation, so a naive carry long without tail hedging misstates risk — not a direct test of the QC rule.
Engel-West argue the rate is near a random walk; this paper claims predictable, structured reversion.
That paper finds the random walk hard to beat on monthly FX; here no random-walk benchmark is reported at all.
Engel-West analytic near-random-walk result is the null this paper claims to beat out of sample; the paper cites it and argues TVP recovers content.
Distance and cointegration pairs on NYSE 1990-2020 fail to beat the market overall, against this paper's high Sharpe claim.
Gold Standard Pairs Trading finds distance and cointegration pairs fail to beat the market benchmark on NYSE 1990-2020, while this paper claims a model-driven edge on six US pairs.
This is the Gatev et al. study whose 1962-1997 result the paper says no longer replicates on 1990-2020 US data.
The chapter defines the textbook pairs rule as a tested-sounding strategy; this paper supplies the negative modern evidence.
That paper derives a square-root impact law from a V-shaped latent liquidity profile; this paper finds log fits better over a wider size range.
That paper's theory makes impact a regularly varying power function of size with exponent rho; this paper's data prefer a logarithmic, more strongly concave form.
Later work finds high LOB forecasting power does not necessarily translate into actionable trading signals; this paper only claims forecast-error superiority, no P&L.
DeepLOB reports the CNN+Inception+LSTM state-of-the-art beats prior LOB models on FI-2010; this paper finds a simple MLP is statistically equivalent to its CNN-LSTM on a different stock and dataset.

Minority-game agent model generates fat tails and clustered volatility from strategic interaction, not from a linear self-exciting intensity; a competing generative explanation for the same stylized facts.
The pre-registered, control-matched SPY test found no strike-local effect at GEX walls; a prediction that G drives amplification is not supported by that test at the index level.
On real-world series cross-validation variants are not uniformly better; N-BEATS uses a single horizon-boundary validation split, which is closer to the weaker procedures that paper cautions about.

LTSF-Linear reports simple linear models beating Transformer forecasters on nine benchmarks; TFT's claim of SOTA versus RNN/Transformer baselines is untested against that linear family in the supplied read.
That paper reports deep multi-task TSMOM beating benchmarks; this one argues deep sequence models often lose to one-layer linear DMS baselines on ordered series.
DeepUnifiedMom's claimed deep-learning edge must clear a linear/naive baseline, which this paper says is often not done.
Deep Momentum Networks' gain over vol-scaled TSMOM needs a same-horizon linear DMS baseline; this paper's finding is the general caution.
The DMN 'more than double' claim is a deep-model gain that this paper's linear-baseline critique would require re-checking.
EXFormer's Transformer edge over a random walk on FX would need to clear a one-layer linear DMS baseline under this paper's argument.
The survey argues linear FF-style factor models leave alpha unexplained and underperform ML; the QC tutorial builds a factor ranking strategy on FF proxies.

That abstract argues Kelly is optimal only under specified conditions when relative-wealth competition matters; this paper assumes absolute-wealth growth maximisation throughout, without addressing relative-wealth objectives.

That paper derives in-sample vs out-of-sample Sharpe replication ratios and warns that fitted predictive models overstate OOS Sharpe; this paper reports a substantially higher OOS Sharpe than the benchmark from a tuned 2-year window, which the replication-ratio caution directly questions.

That paper finds carry and momentum payoffs largely disappear once returns are adjusted for predictability from lagged macro variables; this paper claims out-of-sample Sharpe gains from a learned signal, not directly comparable but in tension.
That entry's regression-based ES backtests require joint VaR/ES modelling; this paper argues a model-independent coverage test needs no joint estimation.

The publication-bias meta-review argues most findings replicate and outperformance persists; this paper says complex low-SR fits replicate poorly (30% in the ten-year case study) - a tension worth flagging, on different universes and methods.

Nine US equity signals with weak in-sample predictability that does not persist out of sample; the review's optimistic persistence fact is for published, mostly high t-stat predictors, not for low-hurdle exploratory signals
That paper finds long-end Treasury forwards react to macro/FOMC surprises; Lucca-Moench find no pre-FOMC effect in fixed income, so the equity drift is separate from the announcement surprise.
The FOMC-cycle paper treats all scheduled meetings alike; if a third of surprises are information shocks with opposite sign, the even-week excess return cannot be a clean policy effect.
Same FOMC-cycle claim in the later SSRN version; same objection — pooling policy and information meetings.

Shows a narrow event window alone does not identify a causal effect; this paper's two-shock sign restriction is exactly the extra structure that paper says is needed, and it is an assumption, not a test.
Argues validation controls only help when they cover a specific failure sub-mode, tempering reliance on any single PBO reading.
That replication of 447 anomalies finds 64% of high-minus-low spreads insignificant in US equities; this paper argues for value and momentum as pervasive premia.
The random-walk/no-predictability view of exchange rates is at odds with the positive carry coefficient claimed here for currencies.
Reports mean-variance being extremely sensitive; here under normality min-variance and min-CVaR coincide, so the disagreement is about non-normal returns
That paper's Twitter-based regARIMA model is claimed to beat random walk out-of-sample for EUR/USD, a class of non-macro predictor that Rossi's survey, written before such work, did not find robust.
Taylor-rule TVP-Bayesian forecasts beat the random walk in 5-8 of 10 currencies; this paper finds structural models broadly cannot beat it on MSE
Twitter regARIMA reported to beat random walk and ARIMA on EUR/USD 1-step MSFE/MAE; claimed edge against the benchmark this paper says is hard to beat
Twitter data reported to enhance intradaily EUR/USD forecasts 'in certain cases'; a different frequency but same random-walk benchmark
The book asserts a long variance swap is a bet on realised volatility with no test; this paper quantifies the premium and shows it is concentrated at the short end, not the term.
Variance swap survey assumes the premium is a property of the contract; this paper shows the term structure of the premium is steeply negative only at short maturity.

A rule-based state filter presented with backtest performance; this paper's result is that rule-search performance of that kind does not survive the data-snooping adjustment and does not repeat out of sample.
Rest-of-day intraday momentum is a timing rule claim on futures; not directly comparable, but it is the sort of single-hypothesis result that this bootstrap discipline would need before being banked.
Finds announcement-window policy-surprise responses large and persistent; this paper argues most policy news arrives between meetings, not at the announcement.
Attributes a material share of the FOMC monthly coefficient to the announcement window, whereas here the announcement surprise is small and the cycle carries the premium.
The 151 book restates that equities earn more on announcement days, while this paper documents accommodation following equity declines, a different timing relation; the book entry is untested.
That paper says the S&P leads yield changes; this paper has forward-rate information forecasting returns and, indirectly, output, so the lead direction and content differ.
That paper rejects the recursive (Cholesky) identification of a monetary-policy VAR, the identification Wu-Xia use in the FAVAR.

The FOMC-cycle paper uses the fed funds rate and the FOMC calendar over 1994-2016 as the policy variable; Wu-Xia argue that rate is bounded and uninformative from 2009, so that sort of cycle study is weakened in the ZLB years.

151:19.5 restates that equities earn higher returns on announcement days; this paper finds policy shocks explain only a small share of output variance but says nothing about announcement-day equity drift — the two are not the same claim and should not be merged.

That paper reports the stock market leads Treasury yields; this Letter is agnostic on causation and treats the curve as a predictor, not a follower — a caution against reading the spread purely as a market signal.
The 2013 paper argues carry payoffs disappear once adjusted for macro predictability; Burnside et al. instead argue they reflect peso risk and cannot be explained by standard factors.

Carry paper finds cross-sectional and time-series predictability from carry; pairs trading's contrarian convergence is a different source of return and the two are not reconciled here - a reminder that not all documented premia are the same animal.
Opposite (short) seagull structure — short OTM put, long ATM call, short OTM call — for the same bullish view with capped upside.
Put ratio backspread has NL>NS (long the ratio); this ratio put spread has NL<NS, the opposite skew of the position.
Carry (2015) reports carry predicts returns in every asset class as a raw signal; this paper says the carry payoff is spanned by lagged macro variables.
8.4 combines momentum and carry assuming both are separate premia; this paper argues the two are the same business-cycle bet in 1994-2002 and only later diverge.
8.2 states carry earns a premium because high-rate currencies appreciate; this paper attributes the carry payoff to macro risk that lagged variables span.
Value and Momentum Everywhere reports momentum as a distinct, robust premium; this paper ties momentum to hedge-fund flows and limits to arbitrage.
The limits-of-arbitrage ETF paper finds persistent deviation of ETF prices from NAV (discount predictive of next-day returns), not the clean immediate-reversion arbitrage the chapter assumes.

The dispersion paper tests the same long-constituent-vol/short-index-vol idea and finds the edge collapsed: 24%/mo 1996-2000, -0.03%/mo 2001-2005. The chapter's claim it 'sizably' works is not supported by that later test.
It is sceptical of single moving-average rules such as 3.11 having forecasting power.
It is likewise sceptical of the two-moving-average rule.
It classes support/resistance pivot rules with the 'unscientific' single-stock rules.
It classes Donchian channel rules with the single-stock rules it doubts.
QC study compares copula vs cointegration and finds the method matters; the book's naive correlation approach is the weaker baseline.
Argues the spread model (copula vs distance) is what matters, not the instrument; the two explanations for pairs profitability are in tension.
The VRP entry's short-vol stance is the mirror of the long strangle; neither is tested in the book.
The book's VRP entry asserts implied usually exceeds realised (sell straddles); the long straddle is the opposite bet, and neither entry tests it.
Same long-near/short-far structure as the futures calendar spread but on options; different instrument and risk.
Futures calendar spread (151:10.2) is the same long-near/short-far shape on futures rather than options; the two are different instruments with different risk drivers.
Bull put ladder is the mirror structure; both are definition-only and untested.
Mirror-image structure with calls/puts swapped; same definition-only status, opposite directional payoff.
Chinese commodity futures evidence that intraday reversal cannot cover costs; a warning for a filtered high-turnover variant.
Chinese commodity futures study finds intraday momentum/reversal cannot cover transaction costs, a caution for a high-turnover weekly contrarian book on futures.
The 155-year S&P MA-timing study finds no statistically significant edge over buy-and-hold.
The pre-registered opening-range-breakout grid on 16 years of futures loses its gross edge after costs, which is the closest tested analogue to a breakout reading of this channel rule
EXFormer (a larger Transformer) is reported to beat the random walk on FX direction; this tutorial does not — but the benchmarks differ (random walk vs SPY).
Leakage-safe, search-aware evaluation finds most LLM/ML strategy discovery does not certify out of sample; consistent with this tutorial's underperformance.
That paper documents higher volatility in high-ETF-ownership stocks; the ETF-pair arbitrage tutorial assumes near-perfect substitution without allowing for tracking-driven mispricing.
The carry paper reports a 4.8% p.a. net-of-spread FX premium; this skewness premium implementation loses money over a decade.
Offers the residual construction as a lower-beta, higher-Sharpe alternative to plain 12-month momentum
That paper attributes S&P excess returns to FOMC-cycle weeks, not to January; a competing calendar explanation.
That rule uses 12-month momentum rather than a single month's seasonality; the two signals are conceptually different.
That 2005 futures paper finds cross-sectional momentum at 3-12 month horizons; this one bets on weekly reversal — opposite sign at a short horizon, possibly consistent at the horizon split.
Chinese commodity futures study finds intraday reversal strategies cannot cover transaction costs — directly relevant to a weekly reversal rule with the same cost concern.
That 2026 backtest-overfitting study finds cross-sectional equity signals fail out of sample after proper diagnostics.
Constant-maturity VIX futures lost ~30%/yr 2006-2013; naive 'high VIX, go long' ignores the roll cost that paper documents.
Attribution of the 2024-2026 gold rally to risk aversion, central banks and de-dollarisation, not the equity-vs-bond yield ratio; the two explanations compete.

That paper finds a static OTM-put overlay costs 1.1pp of CAGR; here the OTM put is bought alongside a short straddle, i.e. used as insurance against the short-vol tail rather than as a standalone hedge.
Out-of-sample diagnostics on simple cross-sectional signals do not persist, against a 16-year in-sample figure like this one.
Overfitting diagnostics find simple cross-sectional signals, momentum included, do not persist out of sample.
Cross-sectional US equity signals of this type show in-sample Sharpe that does not persist out of sample.
Time Series Momentum documents momentum as a time-series (own past return) effect on 58 futures; this is a cross-sectional rank with no supporting numbers.
The Bovespa study uses a formal cointegration screen and reports numbers (16.38% excess, Sharpe 1.34); the distance method here uses no cointegration test and reports none.
That entry screens by correlation then cointegration on 10-minute bars and reports a Sharpe 0.968; this one uses distance only and gives no statistics.
That study finds simple equity signals do not persist out of sample, against this tutorial's unshown factor-selection claim.
That paper finds weak in-sample predictability in simple US equity signals that does not persist out of sample, against this tutorial's unquantified claim of persistence over 60 years.
The copula pairs paper argues copulas beat distance/cointegration selection; this tutorial uses the cointegration approach the copula paper rejects.

EXFormer claims walk-forward FX directional beats a random walk; the HP-trend tutorial is an FX predictability attempt whose own author reports instability — they don't test the same signal but point in opposite directions on FX predictability.
On MNQ/MGC 14 OHLCV momentum/breakout families all fail the five validation gates; consistent with Dual Thrust's negative SPY result.

The pre-registered opening-range breakout study finds breakout profits do not survive costs on 16 years of futures; this tutorial's 2.3% annual return / 0.31 Sharpe does not address costs and is consistent with that null result.
The Bovespa paper reports strong returns from the cointegration method alone; this tutorial claims copulas beat cointegration, i.e. cointegration alone is weaker than reported there.
Time Series Momentum finds 12-month continuation across 58 futures; this paper finds long-horizon contrarian in Chinese equities.
Overfitting diagnostics on nine simple cross-sectional US equity signals find in-sample predictability that does not persist out of sample; this paper's LSTM claim needs the same held-out scrutiny.
Cross-sectional equity signals show weak in-sample edge that does not persist out of sample, the same failure mode to suspect here.
Model-based forecasts failing to beat a random walk out of sample is the opposite direction of evidence.
That paper reports SVM beating other classifiers on Indian index direction; here ML barely edges a random walk.
That paper finds simple cross-sectional signals do not persist out of sample; this one is fitted on the same panel, so the same backtest-overfitting concern applies.
Paper reports mfBm beating HAR and variants out of sample; HAR-RV is the library's long-memory benchmark.
The realized-range efficiency result assumes a continuous semimartingale; this paper shows the plain range statistic is jump-biased, qualifying that result.
Decomposing value finds the value premium concentrated in high-B/M firms that have shrunk (conservative investment), not attributed to distress risk; tension with the distress explanation here.
That paper's seven-check protocol finds apparent crypto perp-futures edges largely collapse under overfitting/beta/collinearity/look-ahead checks, a caution on this paper's reported improvement.
A Century of Evidence finds time-series momentum persists across 67 markets over a century, whereas this paper finds no significant MA-timing edge post-1942 on the S&P.
Across 47 futures the true EWMA-to-future-RV scaling is always below the naive root-h scaling — a caution that simple RV-based benchmarks (and hence IV gains) must be scaled correctly.
Inventory-based expected returns in that paper are conditional on storage state; this one says cycle/policy conditioning has not produced significant, lagged, tested gains.
Gold regime rule is a state-conditioned timing rule of the kind this paper finds insignificant once tested; treat as caution on regime-conditional claims.

Both study commodity index rolls; that paper finds index rolls have little futures price impact and inflows do not move prices, whereas this paper claims significant roll-window price impact and large front-running profits.
Till argues financial investors are liquidity providers, not price distorters; Mou's price-impact/limits-to-arbitrage story is the opposite read.

Time Series Momentum finds broad, persistent time-series momentum across asset classes; this paper finds the currency cross-sectional momentum spread is near zero outside high-RD months — a conditioning result that limits the unconditional-momentum framing.
Carry earns positive returns on high-rate currencies; this paper says the CIP arbitrage allocation is the opposite (borrow high-rate, lend low-rate), so the two returns cannot both be free
Carry returns as a cross-asset premium; this paper implies part of the forward differential is funding/regulatory cost rather than expected depreciation

That paper argues VIX is a useful hedge held long above threshold; this paper's evidence is on the short side of the same complex, not a direct contradiction of the hedging role, but a different sign of the same premium.
The overfitting diagnostic finds cross-sectional US equity signals' in-sample Sharpe does not persist out of sample; that argues for treating IMOM's 47-year in-sample Sharpe above 1 with caution.
Multiple-testing cutoffs from …and the Cross-Section: three style factors across 7 countries x 3 portfolios is a wide search that needs the higher t bar the catalogue argues for

A curve-bucket carry factor with IR 1.0 is claimed to be unexplained by value/momentum; if DNS factor forecasts are as uninformative as shown here, that IR cannot be attributed to forecasting the curve, only to carry/roll exposure.
A curve-carry factor with information ratio 1.0 is exactly the kind of published factor this paper says must be re-judged against a multiple-testing cutoff rather than a single t.
Carry predicting returns in every asset class is a broad family of published findings; Harvey et al. argue the reported t-stats should be discounted for the number of tests.
Currency carry (4.8% p.a., Sharpe 0.54) is a published factor whose significance should be assessed against the multiple-testing bar, not the nominal t.
Volatility-managed portfolios span many factors; the paper's alphas across many factors are the sort of family that a multiple-testing correction would deflate.

Simulation study reporting MVO is 'extremely sensitive' and risk parity more robust; HRP claims to fix the instability by not inverting, and goes further than plain risk parity (IVP) which that paper treats as robust.
Erb-Harvey say gold is not a reliable safe haven; the COVID-phase paper finds gold was a safe haven for equities in Phase I but lost that status — a regime-dependent refinement of the same debate.
On MNQ/MGC 2023-25, none of 14 OHLCV intraday-momentum/mean-reversion families pass the OOS-after-friction gates, suggesting the effect on modern index micro-futures is not tradeable net of costs.

Time Series Momentum shows past returns predict; Koijen et al. report carry remains positive alpha after controlling for time-series momentum, so the door remains open to both signals and carry is not subsumed.
Value and Momentum Everywhere finds value and momentum premia; Koijen et al. find carry produces unexplained alpha after both, implying carry is a separate factor, though not necessarily rival.
14 OHLCV intraday momentum/mean-reversion families on MNQ/MGC; none pass all five validation gates — the US index intraday pattern does not survive in NQ 2023-25 under their tests
That paper links hedge-fund share of open interest to price/positioning effects; Till's review argues positions react to prices, not the reverse.
That paper treats COT PMPU shocks as tradable alpha; Till's lead-lag reading says positioning follows price.
Regime-dependent weights on time-series momentum (MOP 2012, Goulding-Harvey-Mazzoleni) versus this paper's claim that volatility-state dependence is removed by the exit rule alone.
US cross-sectional signals show in-sample predictability that does not persist out of sample; a warning against the size of this paper's reported alphas.

That paper reports wallet-identity features lifting one-second R^2 from 10.88% to 12.31% on DEX perps; this paper reports positive but tiny forward IC on US equities that is swamped by costs — different venue and cost structure, so a direct contradiction is not clean.

The LLM decision model in this paper's Program is exactly the failure mode the other paper reports (validation IC 0.055/0.065 falling to 0.020 on blind 2026); here the LLM result is a sort-order artifact.

The NQ IV-band reversion study reports n=860 with positive exit Sharpe only at VXN extremes; under this paper's logic a low reported PBO on a post-hoc grid would not certify it, and the sample size is below this paper's T=800 only marginally so robustness depends on the search record.

The vGRE overlay's reported 2.34 Sharpe on a two-year NAS100 backtest is exactly the kind of post-hoc grid the paper warns cannot be certified by a low PBO; the paper does not audit it but the caution applies.
Global short-term reversal is reported as significant once properly measured; this paper's reversal features do not survive CPCV out of sample on US stocks.

Pre-registered, control-matched SPY test finds no strike-local GEX-wall effect; both papers test chart-structure levels on index data, and the one that pre-registered and used matched controls found nothing, so vGRE's unreplicated single-sample outperformance reads weaker against it.

The library's carry/ERC paper shows a simple carry-cushion allocation on US Treasuries; this dissertation's own finding is that a calibrated BL overlay fails to beat 1/N or the benchmark - consistent with 'simple beats optimised' rather than a BL edge.
Chinese commodity futures study finds intraday strategies cannot cover transaction costs; this paper charges no costs, so its monthly HML returns are gross and untested against that friction finding.
The pre-registered breakout study finds gross edge does not survive costs on futures; this paper reports long-short factors with no cost charge, so its net-of-friction edge is untested
Not a contradiction of findings, but the GEX engine names concrete instruments, strikes and IV inputs for GC while this paper names no instrument or data at all.

That paper attributes ~33% of the monthly stock coefficient on FOMC surprises to the two-day announcement window; this one finds only the impact-day effect is robust and the post-window drifts reverse, narrowing what monthly regressions can attribute to the window.

That paper prices press-conference-window exposure in the cross-section; this one finds the information/communication component's price effect is one trading day and reverses, arguing against it carrying lasting information.

Its short-VIX-futures FOMC-day effect is a narrow-window claim; this paper shows monthly coefficients are one-and-a-half to three times the window coefficient and cannot be read as mostly window effects.

That paper builds G10 carry from Nelson-Siegel yield-curve factor sorts and claims Sharpe improvement; this one finds NS/DNS factor forecasts add no out-of-sample accuracy over a random walk after 2000, so any NS-factor trading edge would have to come from level, not forecastability.
That paper ties USD/TRY carry returns to crash risk; this one finds no reliable average carry loss or exposure gradient from JGB shocks in its (different) currency set.

Chinese commodity futures paper finds short-horizon reversal dominated by trading frequency; this one finds short-term momentum survives once the trading-flow reversal is partialled out (different market and data).
Meta-labeling paper reports near-0.5 AUC for intraday futures trend filter; this paper argues signal refinement is not where trend-following gains are.
That paper argues the sign of dealer gamma is an inventory assumption, not a Greek (put-call parity); this paper's NetGamma rests on exactly that assumed dealer inventory sign.
Pre-registered SPY test found no strike-local GEX wall effect on price; this paper finds a gamma-liquidity effect, but on single-name spreads, not index prices.

The library's pre-registered, control-matched SPY test found no statistically significant strike-local effect at Rank-1 GEX walls; this engine's wall/pin claims are untested and would have to survive that same design.

That paper proposes (but does not run) strike-local dealer-gamma stabilisation/amplification around heavy-open-interest strikes; this paper's pre-registered test finds no strike-local effect versus controls, arguing against the premise.

NQ paper treats an IV band around prior close as the regime switch; this paper shows the dashboard 'gamma flip' crossing carries no extra vol information beyond net GEX sign, so a flip-level boundary is weakly grounded.
That paper has signature features beating HAR-RV in walk-forward; this one has neural nets (NHITS, TFT, LSTM) losing to HAR on all metrics, a contrary reading of ML's edge on RV.

That G7 study finds no single range estimator consistently improves HAR-RV; this paper claims a data-driven signature feature set does beat HAR-RV, at least intraday, so the two disagree on whether richer features beat the plain HAR baseline.

That paper warns that forecast comparison using an imperfect proxy can select the worse forecaster; here the proxy is 5-bar RV from yfinance bars and no significance test is run, so the RMSE ranking should be read with that caveat in mind.
Claims commodity index investing is not destabilizing; Buyuksahin-Robe find the linkage is about hedge funds, not index traders, and that correlations did rise with hedge-fund share.
Managed-volatility paper reports Sharpe improvements from vol-scaling; Christie's framework implies such improvements need a formal equality test, not just point-estimate comparison, to be trusted.

Pairs-trading paper reports a point Sharpe of 1.34 as evidence of outperformance; Christie's result cautions that a single Sharpe estimate, without a formal distinguishability test against a benchmark, carries large estimation error.

The IV-index review finds broad-based evidence IV predicts realized vol across 71 indices; Fornari-Violi's case-study approach offers much weaker, non-statistical support for similar predictive claims about implied distributions.

That paper treats range-based vol as a robust simple estimator of stochastic vol; this paper argues pure diffusion/stochastic-vol models alone poorly fit short-term skew without a jump overlay, a methodological tension.

Managed-volatility paper finds scaling exposure inversely to vol adds excess return/smooths risk, which is in some tension with a pure negative-risk-premium ICAPM story where high vol exposure should simply earn lower average return rather than be avoidable for free alpha.
that falsification study found no OHLCV-based MNQ/MGC signal survives all validation gates, while this paper claims a surviving NQ vol-band reversion edge -- directly tension-worthy for library.
ORB breakout study found breakouts don't survive costs; this paper's rejected momentum/continuation alternative aligns with that but its reversion claim is the opposite trade direction.

the 225-cell ORB study finds no net-of-cost edge in OHLC-based breakout/range rules on real futures, while this paper's herding mechanism is offered as a theoretical reason volatility clusters but gives no evidence such clustering is exploitable after costs

That paper finds volatility response is asymmetric to prior price direction (falls generate more excess vol, lag-resolved in crypto/equity minute data); this paper instead finds high realized volatility conditions strengthen directional continuation (momentum) rather than simply more range, a differ

themes.label: FX, rates & macro
themes.summary: The strongest material in this theme is carry. Many independent papers agree it pays and that it gives the gains back in volatility spikes, which points to one system: carry, a vol gate and variance sizing. The second cluster is FOMC event timing, where a pre-meeting equity drift and our own validated post-meeting dollar drift fit into one event book. Positioning and funding-basis ideas only work in conditional form, which matches the desk's record (unconditional COT null; release-day crowding and year-end basis validated). Most single-forecast ideas (fundamentals, yield-curve factors, rates leading FX) agree with our nulls that the random walk is hard to beat, so they appear only as low-graded new angles.

blueprints.name: Vol-gated, vol-scaled G10 carry
blueprints.idea: Rank G10 currencies each month by their short-rate gap to the dollar, then go long the top and short the bottom (the classic carry sort). Cut or flatten the book on days when global FX volatility jumps, and scale size by the inverse of last month's realised variance. Give the highest-yielders an extra haircut, because their skew is the most negative.
blueprints.market: G10 FX (7-8 USD pairs plus crosses), CFD-tradeable

parts.why: The base signal: a high-minus-low forward-discount sort earns 4.8% a year net of bid-ask (Sharpe 0.54; developed-only 0.39).
High-rate currencies lose when global FX volatility rises unexpectedly, so a daily vol-shock gate targets exactly the state where carry loses.
Scaling by inverse prior-month variance is reported to add alpha across factors including the FX carry trade, so it fits the same monthly book.
The rate differential predicts negative skew (cross-sectional R2 81%), so a skew-aware haircut on the top-yield names limits the crash tail the gate misses.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: All four parts describe one object: carry is paid for bearing crash risk that arrives with volatility spikes. The direction part collects the premium; the gate and the sizing step aside from the state where the premium is taken back.
blueprints.data_note: OANDA FX M1/daily from 2002 with financing; FRED/OECD short rates (the EUR OECD feed has been dead since 2026-02-16; use German call money as the fx-factor-carry study did); long FRED daily FX for 1976+ as used in rate-diff-xsmom; CVOL/CME IV for an implied-vol gate variant.

evidence.bearing: Plain carry ran an OOS Sharpe of +0.36 with a CI that spans zero, so the base signal is in the published range but unproven here.
A design flaw ran the risk-off gate on carry monthly, so a daily vol-shock gate has never been tested as meant.
The same code ranked by rate level (carry) earned +5.0% a year, Sharpe 0.54, over 1976-2014, which gives a long sample to test the overlays on.
The VIX-gated carry sleeve alone ran Sharpe 0.13 (2013+), so a VIX gate on its own adds little; this test is an FX-vol gate plus variance scaling.

blueprints.risk: Power: with 8 currencies the Sharpe standard error is near 0.4, and decay after publication (P042) may have removed most of the premium since 2008.
blueprints.first_test: On 1976-2026 FRED rates and FX, compare carry with a daily FX-vol-innovation gate plus inverse-variance sizing against the same carry book with no gate and no scaling. Score the Sharpe difference and the worst-month loss with a block bootstrap.

blueprints.name: FOMC two-leg book
blueprints.idea: Leg 1 holds US index longs for the 24 hours before a scheduled FOMC statement and exits just before it (the pre-announcement drift). Leg 2 holds the dollar basket for five sessions after the decision (the desk's validated drift). Leg 2 is split by whether the 30-minute move in rates and stocks says policy shock or information shock.
blueprints.market: NAS100/SPX500 CFDs or NQ/ES futures (leg 1); 7-pair USD basket (leg 2)
blueprints.horizon: event: 24h before the meeting, then 5 sessions after

parts.why: The S&P rose 49bp on average in the 24h before scheduled FOMC meetings (t>4.5), with a Sharpe above 1.1 for the hold-only rule. This is leg 1.
Implied vol ramps into the meeting and drops after it, so leg 1 is an uncertainty premium to hold only up to the statement.
Splits each meeting into a policy shock (rates up, stocks down) or an information shock (rates up, stocks up; 34% of events), giving a state to condition the post-meeting dollar leg.
FOMC surprise effects on the 2y, stocks and FX persist after controls for confounders, which supports a multi-day hold rather than a same-day fade.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: Both legs trade the same scheduled resolution of policy uncertainty: a premium for holding risk into it, then a drift as the decision is absorbed. The shock-type split is the extra state the desk's unconditional post-FOMC drift never used.
blueprints.data_note: Index CFD M1 2016-2026 and NT8 ES/NQ minute data; FOMC calendar; US 2y CFD and index 30-minute moves for the shock sign; OANDA USD pairs for the basket.

evidence.bearing: Leg 2 already exists: +26bp over 5 sessions, 65% positive, +26bp in both halves. It is not yet proven forward.
The FOMC sleeve ran Sharpe 0.95 but its first half was negative, so conditioning may matter.
Statement tone does not predict next-day dollar direction, so condition on the shock sign measured in the market, not on the text.
A rising VIX9D/VIX into events was not shown to add range information, so use the ramp only to time the exit, not as a filter.

blueprints.risk: The pre-FOMC equity drift was measured on 1994-2011 and may have faded since; with about 80 meetings in our window, the leg-1 test is thin.
blueprints.first_test: On 2016-2026 NQ/ES minute data, measure the pre-FOMC return from 14:00 to 13:55 ET the next day across about 80 meetings, net of spread. Benchmark it against the same clock window on non-FOMC days (placebo distribution).
related: Pre-FOMC drift sleeve, flat before the press conference
Pre-FOMC drift with the IV ramp

blueprints.name: Crowded carry fade on release days
blueprints.idea: When leveraged funds are crowded in a currency (a COT extreme) and a high-impact release for that currency lands, trade against the crowd for the session. Weight by carry rank, because speculative positioning piles into high-rate currencies, and by the expected surprise size.
blueprints.market: 6 USD majors

parts.why: Rate differentials predict both negative skew and speculators' net futures positions, so crowded longs sit in high-carry currencies that are prone to sharp falls.
A crowding gauge for carry and trend styles that flagged carry as crowded before the 2008 unwind. It supports conditioning on crowding rather than on raw position.
Shows that unconditional COT direction on four majors is null after costs, so any edge must come from the release-day condition, not from positioning alone.
Financial-customer flow moves FX, and the link is stronger weekly than daily. That fits positioning mattering when an event forces it to be traded.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: A release is the moment that forces crowded, skew-loaded positions to trade as flow, and the carry tilt says which crowds are most fragile.
blueprints.data_note: CFTC TFF/legacy COT 2006+, point-in-time; economic calendar 2014-2026 and the surprise backfill; OANDA M1 bid/ask; policy-rate gaps.

evidence.bearing: The core effect exists: +0.064 ATR against the crowd on release days, positive on 6 of 6 pairs, but only about 3-4 pips on EURUSD before costs.
Unconditional positioning carries no forward information, which matches P086.
Surprise size widens the release session, so it can set trade size.
The crowded-with-trend pullback state is real on futures, a second conditional positioning effect.

blueprints.risk: The validated effect is about 6% of a day's range, so even if a carry tilt doubles it, it may not clear the spread.
blueprints.first_test: Re-run positioning-into-release-direction split by the currency's carry rank (top half vs bottom half), and score the difference in ATR against the crowd using the non-release-day placebo as the benchmark.

blueprints.name: JGB short-end shock carry unwind
blueprints.idea: When the 2-year JGB yield jumps up while global FX volatility is already high, short a basket of high-yield currencies against the yen for five days. Ignore moves in the 30-year JGB.
blueprints.market: AUDJPY, NZDJPY, CADJPY and other high-carry yen crosses

parts.why: Positive short-end JGB shocks hurt carry currencies only when global vol is high (Holm p 0.018 for the interaction).
The effect sits at the 2-year, not the orthogonal 30-year, and the linear average effect is negligible. The trade must therefore be conditional and use the short end only.
Supplies the global FX volatility state that P762's interaction needs, and explains why carry loses in that state.
The currencies with the highest rate differential carry the most negative skew, so they get the largest short weight.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: A rise in yen funding cost at the front end, in a high-vol state, forces carry positions to unwind. Each part names one link in that chain.
blueprints.data_note: The JP curve from 2005 is committed (the flow-chain builds the daily 2y and then drops it from the live store); OANDA yen crosses M1; global FX vol from CVOL/CME IV or realised vol across the majors.

evidence.bearing: The yen firming while US yields rose gave only 35 episodes, too few to score; the desk never tested the JGB 2y trigger with a vol state.
BIS yen-lending growth did not predict squeezes, but that was a quarterly funding stock, not a daily JGB shock.
A foreign-led 10y rise did not give the textbook direction on USDJPY the next session. This design uses the 2y, a vol gate and carry crosses instead.

blueprints.risk: High-vol days with large positive JGB 2y shocks are rare (the BoJ pinned rates near zero for most of 2013-2022), so there may be too few events.
blueprints.first_test: First replicate P762 on our own data: on 2013-2026, regress 5-day returns on the yen-cross carry basket against JGB 2y shocks interacted with a high-FX-vol flag, against a shifted-date placebo.

blueprints.name: Bad-times short dollar
blueprints.idea: Short the dollar against a broad basket when foreign rates sit above US rates on average and US growth is weak. Add to the position after a sharp equity drop between meetings, which implies a coming Fed cut. Size by inverse recent variance.
blueprints.market: USD vs G10 basket

parts.why: Dollar carry timed by the average forward discount and US industrial production forecasts up to 25% of one-year dollar returns and is uncorrelated with standard carry.
A 10% stock fall between meetings predicts a 32bp cut at the next meeting, a timely trigger for a shrinking US rate advantage.
Confirms the dollar is priced as a factor of its own (loading 0.136), separate from carry, so this book is a different bet from blueprint 1.
Inverse-variance scaling for a monthly factor book.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: Bad US states raise the price of risk and the odds of Fed easing, and both point to a weaker dollar against the whole basket, not just the high-yielders. P036's loss in vol spikes applies to high-yielders, which this basket does not overweight.
blueprints.data_note: FRED INDPRO (ALFRED vintages for point-in-time), US and foreign short rates, DTWEXBGS, OANDA USD pairs, index CFDs for the equity drop between meetings.

evidence.bearing: A growth/inflation quadrant found nothing usable for USD at 1-8 weeks. This design is the forward-discount signal at a monthly-to-annual horizon.
Dollar momentum does not continue the next day, so do not expect follow-through at short horizons.
The dollar drifts up after FOMC meetings unconditionally, which may fight a short-dollar leg around meetings.

blueprints.risk: P037's R2 is at a one-year horizon, so a monthly book has few independent observations and long losing spells.
blueprints.first_test: Rebuild P037's dollar-carry signal point-in-time on 1976-2026 FRED data, and score monthly USD-basket returns when the signal is on against always-short-dollar and always-long-dollar benchmarks.

blueprints.name: Treasury curve carry with rate-vol filter
blueprints.idea: Hold the curve segment with the most carry plus roll-down per unit of duration, duration-neutral against the segment with the least. Time the size of the position with the tent-shaped forward factor, and cut it when short-rate volatility is high, because the slope reprices then.
blueprints.market: US Treasury curve via 2y/5y/10y/30y bond CFDs; German curve as a second market

parts.why: Curve carry across 10 bond markets earns a global Sharpe of 0.68 (alpha t=2.7).
One combination of forward rates forecasts 1-year bond excess returns with R2 0.34-0.37, against 0.06 for Fama-Bliss.
Slope and curvature move with conditional short-rate vol, so a rate-vol state signals when the carry ranking is likely to shift.
Nelson-Siegel factor forecasts lose to a random walk, so the system uses raw carry and forward rates, not fitted curve factors.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: The carry and forward-rate signals both read the term premium from today's curve. Rate vol is what moves that premium, so it is a natural risk gate.
blueprints.data_note: US curve 1M-30Y and term premium held; DE/JP curves from 2005; OANDA US 2y/10y CFDs used in earlier studies. Still to check: history and financing for tradeable 5y/30y and Bund CFDs. MOVE committed from 2002.

evidence.bearing: Curve shape failed as a signal for risk assets. This is a signal for bond returns themselves, which the desk has not tested.
MOVE added nothing to Nasdaq vol forecasts, but that says nothing about bond curve trades.

blueprints.risk: On a two-leg duration-neutral book, bond CFD financing and spreads may eat a monthly carry worth only tens of basis points.
blueprints.first_test: On 2005-2026 US and German zero curves, compute monthly duration-neutral curve-carry returns with and without a MOVE-high gate. Benchmark against an equal-weight 2s10s steepener and buy-and-hold 10y.

blueprints.name: Surprise-driven rates drift
blueprints.idea: After a big data or FOMC surprise, hold the bond CFD in the direction of the surprise for one to five days. The premise is that long-end forwards absorb news slowly and the shock persists. Skip the intraday reaction window.
blueprints.market: US 2y/10y bond CFDs; Bund/Gilt as a pooled panel

parts.why: Long-horizon forward rates move on 11 of 13 macro surprises (e.g. payrolls 5.1/3.5/1.9bp per SE at 1y/5y/10y), contrary to models in which shocks fade.
A 1pp FOMC tightening surprise moves the 2y +81bp and the 10y +47bp, and the move persists after controls for confounders.
Separates target surprises from path (forward guidance) surprises, so the drift can be measured per surprise type.
Post-window drifts in monthly FOMC regressions reverse, so the hold should be short and the exit fixed.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: All four papers measure how much of a policy or data surprise stays in rates after the window. The system bets that the window under-prices persistence, and caps the hold where P758 says the move reverses.
blueprints.data_note: Surprise backfill (8 economies, 2007-2025) and ALFRED US first prints; FOMC calendar; OANDA 2y/10y CFD M1; DE/UK 10y (3 years live, longer in the committed curves).

evidence.bearing: Post-release drift on FX and indices was near zero at +1h; rates instruments were not tested.
Following the first 15-minute move did not pay on our instruments, a warning that the drift may not exist.
Market rate surprises did not give EURUSD a direction after the event.
After FOMC, the 2y and 10y gave back the first move as often as after matched non-FOMC days, so there is no special reversal either.

blueprints.risk: P353 measures how much rates move on the day, not a drift afterwards, so the persistence premise may fail beyond the day, as our FX tests found.
blueprints.first_test: Pooled across US releases 2010-2026, measure the signed 10y CFD move from release+30min to +1/+3/+5 days, in sigma per unit of surprise, against a same-clock non-release placebo.

blueprints.name: CIP basis fair-value residual
blueprints.idea: Model the daily cross-currency basis from three public state variables: NFCI, the broad dollar and the 10y-2y slope. Trade only when the actual basis is far from that fair value, expecting the basis to converge and the dollar to move with it.
blueprints.market: EUR, JPY, CHF, GBP vs USD (basis from CME futures vs spot; spot FX leg)

parts.why: NFCI, the broad USD and the slope explain post-GFC CIP deviations with in-sample R2 0.64 and leave-one-year-out R2 0.50.
A 1pp dollar rise goes with a 2.6bp wider basis, so the basis and the dollar share a funding state.
The average G10 basis of 24bp at 3 months persisted after the crisis, which shows how much of the gap is structural cost rather than signal.
In crises, deviations persist for months because of funding limits, so the residual trade must stand aside in stress.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: The basis is the price of dollar funding. The fair-value model strips out the part driven by the state, leaving a residual that is either noise or a mispricing. Crisis periods are excluded.
blueprints.data_note: Basis from CME FX futures vs spot 2016-2026 (the committed CSV is the only copy; not live); NFCI partial; DTWEXBGS and slope held.

evidence.bearing: A raw one-day widening of the basis did not predict USD. The residual from a state model is a different trigger.
A widening basis did not predict FX vol either.
Calendar funding pressure in the basis is real (-14.4bp across year-end), so the model must include a year-end term.
The same year-end premium shows up via CHF (-19.3bp).

blueprints.risk: The basis cannot be traded directly on CFDs, and its link to spot FX was null in our tests, so the residual may forecast only the basis itself.
blueprints.first_test: Fit P248's three-variable model walk-forward on the 2016-2026 basis data. Before attaching any FX leg, test whether the top-decile residual predicts the 5-day basis change, against a shifted-date placebo.

blueprints.name: Slow G10 blend: Taylor value + carry + momentum
blueprints.idea: Combine three slow currency signals in one dollar-neutral book: Taylor-rule fair value, carry and cross-sectional momentum. Turn momentum down in months when returns across currencies are tightly bunched (low dispersion). Rebalance monthly or quarterly.
blueprints.market: G10 FX, ideally plus EM for breadth

parts.why: Taylor-rule forecasts with time-varying parameters beat a random walk out of sample for 5-8 of 10 currencies.
Carry, momentum and value-reversal each add to the optimal currency portfolio (about +0.5 Sharpe on average); real rates and the current account do not.
Currency momentum pays when cross-sectional dispersion is high (1.24% a month) and not when it is low.
Momentum earns up to 10% a year on 48 currencies; this is the third sleeve.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: Value, carry and momentum have low correlation with each other, so the blend is a diversification play. The dispersion gate and the Taylor fundamentals are the parts our earlier stack lacked.
blueprints.data_note: OANDA G10 and Yahoo 19 crosses incl. EM (dormant); US ALFRED CPI. Missing: non-US CPI vintages and output gaps (needs a keyless OECD fetch).

evidence.bearing: Equal-risk carry + momentum + value (5y reversal) + surprise ran a net Sharpe of +0.05 [-1.01, +1.21] on 8 currencies.
Value was a 5-year reversal proxy, not Taylor fundamentals; the Taylor version is untested.
Plain momentum was negative OOS (-0.39); the dispersion gate is the new part.
Time-series trend on FX is null, a caution for any momentum sleeve.

blueprints.risk: P042 reports these FX styles fell from +0.39 to -0.32 Sharpe after publication, and 8 currencies leave the test badly underpowered.
blueprints.first_test: Before building any blend, test the momentum sleeve alone with P690's dispersion gate on 1976-2026 FRED FX (longer sample, more currencies) against ungated momentum.
related: FX carry + momentum gated by global FX vol, on a wider currency set

corroborations.title: Carry pays a premium in FX and beyond
corroborations.finding: Independent samples all find a positive carry return: 1920s-30s sterling crosses, 37 currencies over 1983-2008, 32 currencies over 1996-2008, G10 over 2001-2026, and cross-asset futures. Sizes range from a Sharpe near 0.5 unlevered (P040) and 0.54 net of spreads (P722) to 0.6-0.9 within asset classes (P328, P723).
corroborations.markets: G10 and EM FX; bonds, commodities and equities in the cross-asset version

corroborations.title: Carry's return is paid for crash risk tied to volatility
corroborations.finding: High-rate currencies have negative skew (P335, R2 81%) and lose when global FX vol jumps (P036, P762). Option hedging removes a quarter to a third of the return: P721 goes from 6.5% to 4.8% with a 10-delta hedge, and P048 puts crash premia at most one-third. P040 puts the G10 factor's monthly skew at -1.2.
corroborations.markets: G10 and EM FX, yen crosses

corroborations.title: FOMC days carry an outsized share of returns, and the effects persist
corroborations.finding: Equity returns cluster before and on announcements: 49bp in the 24h before FOMC (P319), and announcement days earn 3.36% of a 6.19% annual premium (P133). Implied vol ramps into the meeting and drops after it (P318), and surprise effects on the 2y, stocks and FX persist after controls (P756). Our post-fomc-usd-drift (validated) fits with effects lasting beyond the window.
corroborations.markets: US equities, Treasuries, USD

corroborations.title: CIP deviations persist and follow the dollar funding state
corroborations.finding: The basis averaged 24bp after the crisis (P695), widens 2.6bp per 1pp rise in the dollar (P130), is largely explained by NFCI, the dollar and the slope (P248/P652), and blew out to 65-70bp after Lehman (P807). Our basis-yearend-premium and basis-yearend-chf (both validated) add the calendar side.
corroborations.markets: G10 cross-currency basis

corroborations.title: Model forecasts rarely beat a random walk in FX and yields
corroborations.finding: Nelson-Siegel loses to a random walk at every maturity (P760). Of 45 significant structural-model comparisons, 43 favour the random walk (P338). Only linear regression beats it on monthly CAD (P651), and the published FX styles decayed after publication (P042). Our residual-reversion-fx (null) and fx-short-term-fair-value (underpowered) agree.
corroborations.markets: G10 FX, US Treasury curve

corroborations.title: Cross-sectional currency momentum exists in long samples
corroborations.finding: Momentum earns up to 10% a year on 48 currencies (P724), and 0.73% a month (t 4.38) on 39 currencies, with most of it in high-dispersion states (P690). It was also positive in 1920-39 (P710). All three are broad samples that include EM; our 8-currency test (fx-factor-momentum) was negative and underpowered.
corroborations.markets: Broad FX incl. EM

contradictions.title: Is the carry premium still there after costs?
contradictions.finding: P722, P356 and P723 report sizeable carry Sharpes. P086 (grade A; four majors, retail costs, daily bars) finds every carry configuration negative (best OOS -0.25), and P042 finds FX style Sharpes fell from +0.39 to -0.32 after publication. The differences are breadth (37 vs 4 currencies), era and cost model.
contradictions.settle: Run the same carry sort on the 1976-2026 FRED sample, split before and after 2008, with 4, 8 and 19 currencies and retail CFD financing, to see whether breadth or era kills it.
contradictions.our_evidence: fx-factor-carry underpowered (+0.36, CI spans zero); rate-diff-xsmom carry-level Sharpe 0.54 over 1976-2014; portfolio-book carry sleeve 0.13 since 2013. The desk leans toward 'small and fading' but the question is not settled.

contradictions.title: Does speculative positioning predict currencies?
contradictions.finding: P335 links speculative positions to carry and crash risk, and P731 (grade A) finds 12-week COT effects in commodity producers. P086 (grade A) finds all six COT methods null on daily FX direction.
contradictions.settle: On the same pairs and horizon, separate unconditional positioning (where nulls are expected) from positioning at moments of forced flow (releases, pullbacks).
contradictions.our_evidence: cot-positioning-factor null (sides with P086 on the unconditional version); positioning-into-release-direction validated and cot-crowding-p5 validated (the conditional effects are real).

contradictions.title: Can fundamentals beat the random walk for FX?
contradictions.finding: Taylor rules with time-varying parameters beat the random walk for 5-8 of 10 currencies (P648, P249). Older structural models almost never do (P338), and P337's survey says predictability is weak and depends on the model.
contradictions.settle: Run a point-in-time Taylor-rule test with real-time CPI and output-gap vintages, scored by a tradeable rank-IC as well as out-of-sample RMSE.
contradictions.our_evidence: fx-short-term-fair-value underpowered and residual-reversion-fx null (both used rate/VIX fair values, not Taylor rules); the Taylor version is untested.

contradictions.title: Where does FOMC information live, and does it last?
contradictions.finding: P757 finds only the press-conference half hour is priced in the cross-section (108bp per event in the Powell era). P756 finds the information component's effect lasts one day and then reverses. P758 says the two-day window holds only about a third of the monthly FOMC sensitivity.
contradictions.settle: On the same meetings, measure what share of the 1-5 day move happens in the statement window, the press-conference window and afterwards, split by policy vs information shock.
contradictions.our_evidence: fomc-range-share context (the statement window carries 21.6% of session variance); post-fomc-usd-drift validated (the dollar keeps moving for 5 sessions), which argues against 'it is all in the window' for FX.

contradictions.title: Pre-FOMC drift in stocks but not in bonds?
contradictions.finding: P319 finds a large equity drift before FOMC meetings with no matching effect in fixed income. P353 finds long-end forwards react strongly to FOMC and macro surprises. So bonds respond to the news but not to the run-up.
contradictions.settle: On the same meetings over 2016-2026, compare the 24h pre-FOMC return on NQ/ES with that on the US 10y CFD, each against same-clock non-FOMC windows.
contradictions.our_evidence: none

contradictions.title: Do JGB yield shocks drive carry unwinds?
contradictions.finding: P762 finds a significant carry loss after short-end JGB shocks, but only in high-vol states. P763 finds the linear average effect negligible by equivalence tests. P084 argues carry indices are close to a random walk, with near-uniform state persistence.
contradictions.settle: Re-estimate on our data with the vol-state interaction pre-registered, so the conditional effect is tested directly rather than read off an average.
contradictions.our_evidence: yen-into-yields context (35 episodes, too few); yen-funding-squeeze-usdjpy underpowered. Neither side taken.

themes.label: Equity intraday & options
themes.summary: The strongest material in this theme is about timing and size on US equity indices, not about reading direction from the order book. Two systems have real support: the noise-band momentum rule (P006), which the desk has already reproduced on SPY and which can now be gated by dealer gamma, and an FOMC calendar sleeve (P319 pre-FOMC drift, timed with P318 IV ramp and P757 press-conference window), which the Evidence Book has never tested on equities. Several papers agree that option prices carry information about future realised vol beyond HAR, and that order flow explains the same-time price move but barely predicts the next one; the desk's own tests side with both. The main disagreements are over intraday momentum on index futures (P725/P716/P006 vs the P871 falsification) and over whether dealer gamma matters at single strikes or only as an aggregate sign.

blueprints.name: Gamma-gated noise-band momentum
blueprints.idea: Trade the P006 noise-band breakout on SPY, ES and NQ as published, but switch it on fully only when the CME dealer book is short gamma, and scale size by vol target. The idea is that short-gamma dealers hedge with the move, so breakouts should run further on those days, while long-gamma days dampen them.
blueprints.market: SPY, ES, NQ (US equity index)
blueprints.horizon: intraday (enter from 10:00 ET at :00/:30, flat by close)

parts.why: Supplies the entry: a break of the 14-day time-of-day noise band from the open, with a VWAP trailing stop and vol targeting (Sharpe 1.33 headline, 0.61 base).
Gives the reason trends persist within the day: hedging demand from dealers short gamma pushes price the same way as the move, across 60 futures markets.
Shows that the early-day move predicts the late-day move most strongly when the first half hour is volatile (R2 3.3% vs 0.6% in the low tercile), a second filter on top of the gamma gate.

Supplies the falsification gates (OOS t, trades per fold, net of friction, year stability, permutation test) that every OHLCV momentum family on MNQ failed, so any gated version must pass the same gates.
Lists backtest bugs (such as exit-day lumping) that inflate Sharpe 2-12x, to check before believing a small improvement from the gate.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: P006 is a trend-continuation rule, and P716 explains continuation through dealer hedging in the same direction as the move; gating on gamma sign tests that mechanism directly. P725 adds a same-day volatility condition that points the same way.
blueprints.data_note: SPY 1-min (IBKR, 2007-), NT8 ES/NQ minute data, CME ES/NQ options OI by strike (2020-10 on) for the gamma sign. The CME book is only about 5% of Nasdaq dealer gamma (gamma-regime-trades note), so the gate is a proxy for SPX dealer gamma.

evidence.bearing: The base rule reproduces on SPY net of costs (Sharpe 1.17), so the direction part stands in-sample.
NQ passes every part (net Sharpe 1.23) but ES misses, so a gate that separates good days from bad is worth testing.
After publication the SPY rule is flat (Sharpe 0.20, wide CI); a gate must be judged on the post-2024 sample too.
Tuning band, days, exit and a pre-open VIX/NR4 filter did not beat the paper's rule; the gamma gate was not in that design space.
Short-gamma days run wider than a same-vol random walk on ES (and NQ), which is the range half of the mechanism.
The close-window slope was not larger on negative-gamma days on NQ; a warning that gamma may not lift the trend part.

blueprints.risk: Gamma sign mostly tracks volatility, which the vol-target already uses, so the gate may add nothing beyond the sizing (as gex-range-iv found IV absorbs most of the gamma range effect).
blueprints.first_test: Split the existing NQ/ES/SPY noise-band daily net P&L from 2020-11 by CME gamma sign (OI date D used on session D+2) and test short-gamma minus long-gamma bp/day against 1,000 shuffled gamma labels, with the ungated rule as the benchmark.

also.name: Late-day index momentum on volatile mornings
NQ noise-band momentum timed by first-half-hour volatility

blueprints.name: Pre-FOMC drift sleeve, flat before the press conference
blueprints.idea: Go long ES/NQ about 24 hours before a scheduled FOMC statement and exit just before the statement, so the trade holds the pre-announcement drift but not the announcement and press-conference variance. Size by forecast vol.
blueprints.market: ES, NQ futures (also SPX500/NAS100 CFDs)
blueprints.horizon: event, about 24 hours (14:00 ET day before to 13:55 ET meeting day)

parts.why: Supplies the edge: the S&P rose 49 bp on average in the 24 hours before scheduled FOMC meetings (1994-2011, t above 4.5, Sharpe above 1.1 for hold-only-pre-FOMC).
Shows implied vol rising into the meeting and dropping after, which marks the pre-meeting window as the time risk is priced and the meeting as the release point to exit.
Shows the press-conference half hour (14:30-15:30) carries the priced FOMC-day risk, so being flat before 14:00 keeps the trade out of the biggest variance.
Places the pre-FOMC drift inside a wider pattern: top macro announcement days earn a large share of the equity premium (11-16 bp a day).

blueprints.mechanism_fit: All four papers describe one premium: equity investors are paid for holding risk into a scheduled resolution of uncertainty, and the premium accrues before the release while IV is high. Exiting before the statement takes the drift and avoids the release jump.
blueprints.data_note: NT8 ES/NQ minute bars, NAS100/SPX500 M1 bid/ask 2016-2026, FOMC calendar, VIX/VIX9D for sizing.

evidence.bearing: The window before a tier-1 US release (FOMC included) runs about 12% narrower than matched days, so a drift held in that window carries low variance.
There is no extra drift after a Fed-day vol crush, which supports exiting at the event rather than holding through.
The statement and press-conference windows carry a large share of FOMC-day variance (21.6% vs 2.6% for the statement half hour), the variance this sleeve avoids.
A related FOMC calendar drift holds in the dollar, but this is a different asset and a post-meeting window.
Sets the bar: a 1-day NQ direction cell must move P(up) about 6 pp above the 0.554 base rate to count.

blueprints.risk: The pack's numbers stop at the papers' samples (to 2011), and with about 80 meetings since 2016 a drift much smaller than 49 bp will not be distinguishable from zero.
blueprints.first_test: Hold long ES and NQ from 14:00 ET the day before to 13:55 ET on each scheduled FOMC day 2016-2026 net of futures costs, and compare the mean return with the same 24-hour clock window on all non-FOMC days (block bootstrap and date-shift placebo), benchmark = buy-and-hold per-day return.
