related: FOMC two-leg book

blueprints.name: Priced event jump for FOMC/CPI/NFP range lines
blueprints.idea: Read the market's priced jump for a scheduled release from the option term structure (the extra variance in the expiry that spans the event) and use it to widen the event-day range lines and stops. This replaces the historical typical release size, which failed live.
blueprints.market: ES, NQ (SPX/NDX options for the jump), US index CFDs

parts.why: Shows an explicit scheduled jump for FOMC, CPI and NFP lowers held-out SPX option pricing error (MAE 7.92 to 7.26), so the priced jump can be separated from ordinary vol.
Shows the IV surface ramps into FOMC and the FOMC dummy improves IV prediction, giving the shape of the run-up the lines must follow.
Shows implied vol (VIX) adds to lagged realised vol for RV forecasts (RMSE down 9.15% out of sample), the general case of using priced information.
Places most of the FOMC-day variance in the press-conference window, telling which clock hours the widened line should cover.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: All four say option prices know about scheduled event risk before it happens; P316 gives a way to measure the event part on its own, which is the piece the desk's event layer lacked.
blueprints.data_note: CME settlement IV for ES/NQ per expiry (6 years) and VIX9D/VIX are held; SPX per-expiry chains only from the Cboe intraday log (2026-11 on), so the historical test must use CME expiries.

evidence.bearing: A correction from the typical size of the release type passed in-sample but did not replicate live; this design swaps the historical size for the priced jump.
A rise in VIX9D/VIX before the event did not clearly widen the event day; the jump term uses the expiry structure, not the ramp.
The front of the IV curve already sorts days by how often they pass the p75 line, so priced front-end information is proven useful for range.
Implied vol from CME settlements beats HAR on 7/7 instruments, the base the event term would add to.
The realised release session does scale with surprise size, so there is event variance to forecast.

blueprints.risk: The chosen lines (persistence + IV) may already carry the priced jump through the front IV, leaving nothing extra, as one-range-forecast found for other flags.
blueprints.first_test: On FOMC/CPI/NFP days 2020-2026, compare the pinball loss of NQ/ES H-L lines widened by the CME expiry-spanning jump variance against the production persistence + IV lines, with the event-layer bar of 0.99.
related: Pre-FOMC drift with the IV ramp

blueprints.name: Overnight gap risk sizing for the NQ hold
blueprints.idea: Size the overnight NQ hold (or set its stop) from a forecast of the overnight gap: HAR on gaps plus VXN, plus the dealer gamma level only in calm-VIX regimes. The goal is steadier risk on the overnight leg, not a new direction.
blueprints.market: NQ, ES (NAS100/SPX500 CFDs)

parts.why: Finds SPX dealer gamma adds out-of-sample information on overnight gap size beyond HAR, but only in calm regimes (CW +5.82 calm vs +0.76 stress).
Shows VIX adds to lagged RV in vol forecasts, so the baseline must include implied vol before gamma is credited.
Regime-switching HAR improves RV forecasts, backing a model that changes behaviour between calm and stress states as P079 needs.
Shows a dynamic hedge drags less than static puts (-0.4% vs -1.1% a year), pointing to sizing or dynamic cover rather than permanent options for gap risk.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: In calm markets dealers long gamma dampen moves, so their book should tell how big the overnight gap can be; HAR and VIX give the base vol, and sizing turns the forecast into steadier risk.
blueprints.data_note: NT8 NQ/ES minute, VXN/VIX family, CME NQ/ES OI by strike (2020-) are held; SPX dealer gamma as used by P079 is not, and the CME book is a small share of index dealer gamma.

evidence.bearing: The overnight NQ hold makes +0.034% a trade net, t 2.0, failing Holm, so the trade exists but is thin.
Risk-adjusted overnight return is flat across vol regimes, so sizing by forecast vol should steady risk without killing return.
The closest test of P079's calm-regime idea, on next-session range not the overnight gap, was positive but underpowered; IV absorbed 59% of it.
On ES the calm-regime gamma effect vanished once IV was in the baseline.
Sizing by forecast sigma steadies risk; this blueprint applies it to the overnight leg.

blueprints.risk: Our CME gamma proxy may be too small a slice of index dealer gamma to reproduce P079's SPX result.
blueprints.first_test: Forecast squared NQ overnight return (16:00 to 09:30 ET) 2020-11 to 2026-08 with HAR, HAR + VXN and HAR + VXN + CME gamma, scored by Clark-West against HAR + VXN on calm-VIX days only.

blueprints.name: FOMC-cycle even-week beta
blueprints.idea: Hold vol-targeted ES/NQ long only in even weeks of the FOMC cycle (weeks 0, 2, 4, 6 after a meeting) and sit in cash in odd weeks. The test is whether this timing beats a vol-matched buy and hold, not just plain buy and hold.
blueprints.market: ES, NQ, SPX500/NAS100

parts.why: Finds the S&P excess return 1994-2016 was earned in even FOMC-cycle weeks (+12 bp a day vs odd weeks).
Earlier version of the same study (1994-2013) with the same result; it is not independent support.
Links the premium to scheduled announcement days, a related calendar of equity returns.
Splits FOMC surprises into policy and information shocks (34% information), which may explain which cycles pay and which do not.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: The even-week pattern is read as Fed communication arriving on a biweekly rhythm and lowering risk premia; announcement-day premia and the policy/information split describe the same channel.
blueprints.data_note: NQ/ES daily and NT8 minute, FOMC calendar, VIX for vol targeting.

evidence.bearing: Going flat on VIX-stress days only cut exposure, not risk-adjusted return, so any calendar switch must beat a vol-matched hold.
Vol-target sizing is the fair benchmark for a timing sleeve.
The desk's core beta sleeve already exists; the even-week gate would be an overlay on it.
After FOMC days give-back and continuation rates match non-FOMC days, so no post-meeting reversal undermines week 0.

blueprints.risk: The two papers are one study; the pattern may have faded after 2016, and the post-2016 sample has fewer than 90 cycles.
blueprints.first_test: Compute even-week minus odd-week daily NQ and ES excess return 2017-2026 (after the paper's sample), with a block bootstrap and shifted-calendar placebo, benchmark = vol-matched buy and hold.

also.name: FOMC-cycle timing on the index beta sleeve

related: Pre-FOMC drift with the IV ramp

blueprints.name: Late-day index momentum on volatile mornings
blueprints.idea: Trade the last half hour in the direction of the first half hour (or the rest of day) only when the first half hour was in its top volatility tercile. The paper's own split puts most of the effect there.
blueprints.market: ES, NQ, SPY

parts.why: First half-hour return predicts the last half hour on SPY (slope 6.94, R2_OS 1.4%), with R2 3.3% in the high-vol tercile.
Ties the late-day move to hedging demand across 60 futures, a mechanism that should be stronger on volatile days.
Independent market (Chinese commodity futures) where out-of-sample R2 is positive mainly in the high-volatility subsample.
Sets the cost and stability gates that intraday momentum on MNQ failed.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: All three direction papers point to a high-vol condition, so the filter is the part not yet tested here.
blueprints.data_note: NT8 ES/NQ minute 2016-, SPY 1-min 2007-.

evidence.bearing: The unconditional close-window and first-half-hour slopes are null on NQ and ES, with CIs ruling out the paper's size.
The negative-gamma split was also null on NQ; the vol-tercile split has not been run.
A fast start predicts a wider rest of day, but not a trend-day close, which hints the high-vol filter adds range more than direction.

blueprints.risk: The unconditional null is tight, so the top tercile would need about three times the average slope to show.
blueprints.first_test: Re-run the close-window-momentum regression on NQ/ES 2016-2026 inside the top first-half-hour volatility tercile only, against the same 200-shift placebo and the paper's 6.94 slope as the bar.

also.name: Gamma-gated noise-band momentum
NQ noise-band momentum timed by first-half-hour volatility

related: High-vol intraday hedging-demand momentum on futures

blueprints.name: VXN-extreme band fade on NQ
blueprints.idea: Fade NQ moves that pass the VXN/16 band around the prior close, but only when VXN is very low or very high, with a 30-minute time exit. The paper finds the fade pays only at those extremes.
blueprints.market: NQ futures

parts.why: Moves beyond the VXN band revert 85.2% of the time (n=860); 30-minute exit Sharpe positive only at VXN below 20 (0.38) or 30 and above (0.64).
Low dealer gamma worsens next-day liquidity, a reason the fade could behave differently by gamma state.
Range-expansion reversal failed its gates on MNQ (T -11.52), a direct warning for this fade.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: Reversion beyond a priced band is a long-gamma, liquidity-provision story, so VXN and gamma state are the natural switches; the parts fit but the evidence is mixed.
blueprints.data_note: NT8 NQ minute, VXN daily, CME NQ OI for gamma sign.

evidence.bearing: Fading the p75 line on long-gamma NQ days lost money after costs; this is close to the same trade.
Reaching the median band raises the odds of reaching the next band, which leans against reversion.
Fading stretched touches of v3 lines was not supported.
Band fades on daily FX/gold bars failed; different market and horizon, but the same idea.

blueprints.risk: The VXN-extreme cells are small, and our line-fade tests on NQ already lose after costs.
blueprints.first_test: On NQ 2016-2026, fade the first VXN/16 band break with a 30-minute exit in the VXN below 20 and at or above 30 buckets only, net of real costs, against random-time entries of the same side and hold.

also.name: NQ IV-band reversion only at VXN extremes

blueprints.name: Jump-model regime switch with dynamic tail cover
blueprints.idea: Hold vol-targeted ES/NQ beta, switch to cash when a two-state jump model (with persistence penalty) reads the bear state, and use a dynamic rather than static put hedge. The bar is vol-target alone, not buy and hold.
blueprints.market: ES, NQ, SPX500

parts.why: The jump model beat buy and hold and an HMM on S&P 500, DAX and Nikkei out of sample (S&P Sharpe 0.68-0.71 vs 0.48), net of costs, with 1-10 day delays.
A simple 200-day rule improved Sharpe on a leveraged ETF (0.732 vs 0.572), a cheap benchmark switch.
Dynamic hedging cut 2008 drawdown to -35.1% at -0.4% a year drag, versus -1.1% for static puts.
Protective puts earned 2.5% vs 5.8% a year for the index, so permanent option cover is costly.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: All four aim to cut exposure in sustained bear states; the jump model's persistence penalty is the new part versus HMM tests.
blueprints.data_note: NQ/SPX daily from 2004, VIX family, CME settlement IV for hedge cost.

evidence.bearing: A VIX-stress half-size rule did not add to vol targeting; the regime switch must beat this.
The drawdown cut from going flat was just less exposure once vol-matched.
HMM states did not call direction; the jump model differs by its persistence penalty.
Vol targeting already lowers drawdown (-35% vs -55% on NQ), the benchmark to beat.

blueprints.risk: Like the VIX stress filter, the switch may only lower exposure and lose to vol targeting once matched for risk.
blueprints.first_test: Fit the two-state jump model walk-forward on NQ daily 2004-2026 with a 1-day delay and compare net Sharpe with vol-target-only NQ, vol-matched, with block bootstrap.

corroborations.title: Option prices improve realised vol forecasts beyond HAR
corroborations.finding: VIX cuts 21-day RV forecast error 9.15% out of sample (P781); options-implied rough-Heston vol beats RV-only models (P667); dealer gamma adds to HAR for overnight gaps in calm regimes (P079); the FOMC dummy improves IV prediction (P318); and an explicit event jump improves SPX option pricing (P316). The desk agrees: iv-forecast (validated) and forecast-pick (validated, persistence + IV chosen).
corroborations.markets: S&P 500 / SPX options; desk replication on FX, gold and US indices

corroborations.title: Order flow explains the same-time move but barely predicts the next
corroborations.finding: OFI explains 65-76% of 10-second mid-price changes (P090, P262) and log-GOFI up to 86% (P267, P595), but these are same-time fits. Predictive tests give tiny ICs: +0.0044 swamped by costs (P735) and median 0.009 with nothing surviving FDR (P085). The desk's orderflow-lead (NQ) and orderflow-lead-aggressor (6E/6J) are powered nulls, and flow-range-flow finds only a 0.2% gain on next-hour range.
corroborations.markets: Single stocks (US, China), US ETFs, FX, desk NQ/6E/6J futures

corroborations.title: The FOMC calendar carries an equity premium
corroborations.finding: Equities earn outsized returns in the 24h before FOMC (49 bp, P319), on top macro announcement days (11-16 bp a day, P133), in even FOMC-cycle weeks (+12-14 bp a day, P348/P714, one study in two versions), and through the press-conference window (P757). All are in-sample and none net of costs. The desk has not tested any of the equity versions; it has validated a dollar drift after FOMC (post-fomc-usd-drift).
corroborations.markets: S&P 500, US single stocks

corroborations.title: HAR is hard to beat with complex models
corroborations.finding: HAR beats NHITS, TFT, LSTM and GARCH on RMSE and QLIKE (P777); the HAR cascade beats ARFIMA and AR (P717); fitting HAR with QLIKE is the gain that pays (P779); and in limit-order-book forecasting a simple MLP matches deep nets (P265). The desk agrees: vol-layer-state-confirm-nudge found HAR-month and HARQ add only 0.16%.
corroborations.markets: Equity index, single stocks, FX (USD/CHF), LOB data

corroborations.title: Dealer gamma does not create special price levels
corroborations.finding: A pre-registered SPY test finds Rank-1 GEX walls no different from rank 2-5 nodes (P774); the gamma sign is an inventory assumption, and the flip crossing adds no vol information beyond net GEX sign (P775); the open GEX engine runs no predictive test (P773). The desk agrees strongly: wall-placebo, level-local-gamma, swing-walk-gamma-strike and gamma-regime-trades are nulls, while the aggregate sign does predict range (gex-range-es validated).
corroborations.markets: SPY/SPX; desk NQ, ES, FX, gold CME books

contradictions.title: Does intraday momentum survive on index futures?
contradictions.finding: P725 and P716 find the early or rest-of-day return predicts the last half hour, and P006 builds a profitable SPY breakout rule. P871 finds none of 14 OHLCV intraday momentum or reversal families on MNQ passes OOS and cost gates.
contradictions.settle: Separate the two signals: the close-window slope (P725/P716) and the noise-band breakout (P006) are different trades, so each needs its own post-2020 futures test net of costs with the P871 gates.
contradictions.our_evidence: close-window-momentum null (sides with P871 for the close-window signal); noise-area-momentum-spy validated and noise-area-momentum underpowered (partly with P006); noise-area-momentum-spy-post underpowered

contradictions.title: Does dealer gamma matter for price?
contradictions.finding: P079 finds gamma forecasts overnight gaps in calm regimes, P716 ties momentum to hedging demand, and P771 links low gamma to wider spreads. P774 finds no strike-local wall effect and P775 says the sign is an assumed inventory, not a measured fact.
contradictions.settle: Treat aggregate gamma sign (a vol and liquidity state) separately from strike levels, and test whether the sign adds anything once implied vol is in the baseline.
contradictions.our_evidence: gex-range-es validated (aggregate sign predicts range); wall-placebo null and level-local-gamma null (sides with P774 on strikes); gex-range-iv underpowered (IV absorbs most of the sign)

contradictions.title: Do moves beyond a vol band revert or continue?
contradictions.finding: P850 says NQ moves past the VXN/16 band revert 85.2% of the time, with profit only at VXN extremes. P006 trades the opposite way (follow a band break), and P871 finds range-expansion reversal fails badly on MNQ (T -11.52).
contradictions.settle: Run fade and follow on the same band, same NQ sample and same costs, split by VXN bucket, against random entries.
contradictions.our_evidence: band-reach-from-here validated (reaching a band raises odds of the next, leaning to continuation); gamma-regime-trades null; noise-area-momentum underpowered on NQ but positive

contradictions.title: Is the FOMC cycle a clean policy effect?
contradictions.finding: P348/P714 pool all scheduled meetings and find returns in even weeks. P323 shows 34% of FOMC surprises are information shocks where rates and stocks move together, so pooled meetings mix two opposite signals.
contradictions.settle: Split the even-week return by whether the last meeting was a policy or information shock (P323 sign rule on the 30-minute 2y and S&P move) and check the even-week effect holds in both.
contradictions.our_evidence: none

contradictions.title: Can richer models beat HAR for realised vol?
contradictions.finding: P780 finds signature features slightly beat HAR (RMSE 0.1824 vs 0.1864); P777 finds neural nets lose to HAR on every metric. P232 argues HAR's long memory is really rough vol (H about 0.1), while P717 builds on long memory.
contradictions.settle: Compare on the same assets with a proper loss (QLIKE) and a Diebold-Mariano test; P780 ran no significance test on a noisy proxy.
contradictions.our_evidence: vol-layer-state-confirm-nudge context (HAR extras add 0.16%); forecast-pick validated (persistence + IV beats HAR-800)

contradictions.title: Late-day momentum for the index vs late-day reversal for stocks
contradictions.finding: P725/P716 find the index keeps moving the same way into the close. P049 finds single stocks that lost intraday beat winners over the last half hour (3.05 bp a day out of sample, pre-registered). Both can be true (index trend, stock-level reversal), but they argue for opposite trades in the same window.
contradictions.settle: Test both on the same days: index last-half-hour sign vs cross-sectional loser-minus-winner return, to see if they are independent.
contradictions.our_evidence: close-window-momentum null (no index momentum into the close on NQ/ES); single-stock reversal untested

themes.label: Volatility & regime
themes.summary: The vol papers agree on one thing the desk has already proven: vol is forecastable and implied vol is the best single input, but vol and regime reads almost never give direction. The strongest systems therefore use vol as the forecast, the size, the stop or the on/off switch, around a carry or event premium that comes from somewhere else (VIX futures roll, the pre-FOMC drift, trend). The two best untested ideas are a basis-timed short-VIX-futures carry with a term hedge, and a jump-model regime switch on the index judged against a vol-matched benchmark. Several pack ideas (HMM direction, VIX stress stand-aside, vol-managed Sharpe gains, gamma regimes, fade-in-regime) already sit as nulls or underpowered in the Evidence Book, so they appear only with a stated new angle.

blueprints.name: Basis-timed short VIX futures with a term hedge
blueprints.idea: Short the front VIX future only when the futures basis (contango versus spot) is steep, because the basis forecasts the future's fall, not spot VIX. Hedge part of the tail with a long position further out the curve, the way the combined VIX ETN portfolios do, and size by the vol of the spread. Exit when the basis flattens or inverts.
blueprints.market: VIX futures (VX), with SPX/NQ as context
blueprints.horizon: daily signal, holds of days to weeks

parts.why: States that the VIX futures basis forecasts the futures price change (mean reversion of the future), not the VIX, and gives a roll threshold (0.10 in / 0.05 out) to short UX1.
The Calvados contango rule: shorting only when the daily roll is in contango, with a hedged variant that cut max drawdown from 29.7% to 18%.
Shows the roll cost that makes the short side pay: constant-maturity one-month VIX futures lost about 30% a year 2006-2013, worse at the front than at five months.
Combined long-medium / short-front VIX ETN portfolios (CVIX Sharpe 1.19, CVZ 1.31) give the term-hedge structure that caps the short-front tail.
The variance risk premium is mostly negative, mean-reverting (half-life 38-138 days) and term-structure shaped, which is why the front is where the premium sits.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: All parts describe the same thing: holders of VIX exposure pay a roll premium that is steepest at the front and visible in the basis. The basis times entry, the curve hedge handles the tail, and none of it needs a direction call on the S&P.
blueprints.data_note: VIX futures settles 2013 onward, spot VIX/VIX3M/VIX9D/VVIX from the Cboe family (VIX from 1990).

evidence.bearing: Shorting VX on the ratio flag made +0.22R per trade but random-entry shorting made +0.12R, so the flag beat random by an unproven +0.10R; the edge is mostly roll, which this blueprint targets directly.
The VIX give-back is partly capturable on VX futures (about 60% of spot), but the worst trade lost 54.5%, which is why a term hedge is a required part, not an extra.
A second, independent timing input (VIX moving far more than Nasdaq) that can be tested as a filter on top of the basis rule.
High implied over realised has led to wider indices, not calmer ones, so a short-vol rule must not use a high VRP as its entry trigger.

blueprints.risk: The roll premium is paid for crash risk: a single 2018 or 2020 style spike can wipe out years of carry, and the hedge may cost most of the premium.
blueprints.first_test: From 2013, short the nearest VX with 35+ days left only when its basis to spot is above a threshold fixed in advance, hedged with a long 4-5 month VX; compare net R per trade against the same hedged short on random days (the short-vx-rule benchmark).

blueprints.name: Leverage-aware vol forecast for index sizing and stops
blueprints.idea: Add the pieces the papers say a plain HAR misses, downside semivariance (leverage effect) and the overnight return, to the desk's chosen sigma with IV, and fit it under QLIKE loss. Use the forecast to size index trades and to set stop width, so stops widen after equity falls when realised vol runs above the shipped lines.
blueprints.market: NQ, ES, SPX500, NAS100 (then FX majors as a check)
blueprints.horizon: daily forecast, used for intraday and overnight positions

parts.why: Adding the VIX level to a lagged-RV forecast of 21-day S&P realised vol cut out-of-sample RMSE 9.15%; this is the IV base the desk already ships.
HAR with leverage effects and realised semivariance forecasts better out of sample on Nikkei futures and spot; asymmetric jumps add nothing.
On G7 indices the overnight return vol is the most consistent single addition to HAR, while no range estimator dominates.
Fitting HAR under QLIKE rather than squared error gives significantly better QLIKE out-of-sample forecasts, so fit and score on the same loss.
Across 47 futures the true EWMA-to-future-RV scaling is always below sqrt(h), so the forecast needs horizon-specific scaling before it sets size.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: Leverage and overnight terms both target the same known gap: vol jumps after falls and overnight, which a symmetric close-to-close HAR under-reads. QLIKE fitting and correct horizon scaling make the forecast usable for size and stop width.
blueprints.data_note: NT8 ES/NQ minute data, index CFD M1 2016-2026, VIX/VXN/VIX9D, CME settlement IV; the chosen sigma and forecast history the desk already stores.

evidence.bearing: After a 5-day S&P fall or VIX rise, index ranges exceed the shipped IV-adjusted forecast by about 13%, the exact gap a semivariance term should close.
Index ranges beat the forecast by +6.6% after 20-day S&P falls, again pointing at a missing leverage term.
HAR+IV beats HAR on 7/7 instruments, so IV stays the base and the new terms must add beyond it.
HAR-month and HARQ terms added only 0.16% pinball, so extra HAR terms alone are not enough; the new angle is the asymmetric (downside and overnight) terms.
Sizing by any forecast sigma steadies risk but which sigma is used barely matters for Sharpe, so the payoff should be judged on stops and lines, not on returns.

blueprints.risk: The validated forecast-miss terms may already capture most of the leverage effect, leaving a gain below the 0.5% bar the desk uses.
blueprints.first_test: Walk-forward 2020-2026 on the six indices: chosen sigma plus downside semivariance and overnight squared return, fit under QLIKE, versus the chosen sigma with the validated forecast-miss terms; pass only if pinball improves at least 0.5% with both halves better.

blueprints.name: Jump-model index switch, vol-matched
blueprints.idea: Fit a two-state statistical jump model on daily index returns and hold the index in the calm state, cash in the turbulent state, with a 1-5 day delay. Size the held position by an IV-aided vol forecast. Judge it only against buy-and-hold scaled to the same volatility, because the desk has shown that cutting exposure alone fakes a drawdown gain.
blueprints.market: NQ and ES futures (SPX from 1990 for the long check)

parts.why: Grade-A OOS 1990-2023: the jump-model switch lifts S&P Sharpe from 0.48 to 0.68-0.71 and beats the HMM benchmark (0.51-0.55), even with a 10-day delay.
Grade-A alternative: a three-state HMM expected-Sharpe score used to size futures, which gives a graded size instead of a 0/1 switch to test side by side.
The VIX-aided RV forecast sets position size inside the calm state.
Inverse-variance scaling is the obvious rival to a regime switch; it must be beaten, not just matched.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: The jump model penalises switching, so it targets persistent turbulent spells, the same thing vol clustering produces, rather than one-day stress readings. Vol sizing and the regime switch both act on risk, so they are tested as rivals and as a pair.
blueprints.data_note: NT8 NQ/ES futures (NQ daily 2004 onward used in the stress-filter tests), VIX from 1990, SPX daily history.

evidence.bearing: Going flat on VIX p80 days cut drawdown only through less exposure (-57% vs -55% once vol-matched), so the jump model must beat a vol-matched hold.
Inverse-variance sizing on NQ gave Sharpe 0.622 vs 0.628 and worked 2004-14 then reversed; this is the benchmark arm.
The HMM vol state did no better than an ATR percentile at picking intraday rules; the new angle is the jump model's switching penalty and a multi-week hold, not an intraday rule picker.
A VIX stress state added nothing on top of vol targeting, a strong prior that the jump switch also adds nothing beyond vol targeting.

blueprints.risk: The jump model's gain may be the same 'less exposure in bad times' effect that vanished in the desk's vol-matched stress-filter tests.
blueprints.first_test: NQ 2004-2026 and SPX 1990-2026, jump model refit yearly with a 1-day delay, net of futures costs: Sharpe difference versus vol-target sizing and versus vol-matched buy-and-hold, block bootstrap, bar +0.15.

also.name: Index beta switched by a jump-model regime, vol-managed

blueprints.name: Pre-FOMC drift with the IV ramp
blueprints.idea: Hold the index long for the 24 hours before scheduled FOMC statements, sized by implied vol. Use the rise in short-dated IV into the meeting as the measure of event risk being paid for, and check whether the FOMC-cycle even-week effect adds a second sleeve.
blueprints.market: ES and NQ futures, SPX500 CFD
blueprints.horizon: intraday to one day, around 8 meetings a year

parts.why: S&P rose an average 49bp in the 24 hours before scheduled FOMC statements (1994-2011, t above 4.5), a hold-only rule with Sharpe above 1.1.
S&P implied vol rises monotonically into FOMC with short-dated options moving up to two days before, so the IV ramp times and measures the risk being held.
Only press-conference exposure (14:30-15:30) is priced in Powell-era FOMC-day returns, which tells where to stop holding.
S&P excess return over 1994-2016 came entirely in even weeks of FOMC-cycle time (+12bp a day), a second calendar sleeve on the same mechanism.
Announcement days carry 55% of the equity premium (1961-2014), supporting a risk-compensation reading of the pre-FOMC return.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: All parts say the equity premium is paid around scheduled Fed risk, and the IV ramp is the price of that risk, so IV can size the hold. The exit at the press conference matches where the papers find the priced exposure.
blueprints.data_note: NT8 ES/NQ minute data, index CFD M1 2016-2026, FOMC dates in the calendar files, VIX9D/VIX for the ramp.

evidence.bearing: The front-ratio ramp into events adds little to event-day range and was negative for FOMC; here the ramp is a size input on a return, not a range input.
The pre-release window on tier-1 days is narrower than normal, which fits a quiet pre-FOMC hold with a small stop.
A related post-FOMC dollar drift stands; the equity pre-FOMC drift itself has no entry in the book.
The press-conference hour carries a large share of FOMC-day range, consistent with exiting before it.

blueprints.risk: With about 80 meetings since 2016 the test is small, and the effect may have faded after publication.
blueprints.first_test: ES/NQ 2016-2026 (and SPX daily back to 1994 for power): return from 14:00 ET the day before to 13:55 ET statement day, versus the same clock window on non-FOMC days, placebo-dated, net of costs.

blueprints.name: Multi-asset trend with a panic-state brake
blueprints.idea: Run vol-scaled time-series momentum across futures, but cut or flip exposure in 'panic' states (after a market fall with high vol), where momentum crashes happen. Use regime-specific weights instead of a fixed +1/-1, and do not add trailing stops.
blueprints.market: multi-asset futures (indices, bonds, FX, gold, commodities)

parts.why: Time-series momentum across 71 futures 1974-2012 with risk-scaled Sharpe above 1.2 at monthly, weekly and daily frequency.
Momentum crashes are forecastable: they come in panic states after falls with high vol, and a dynamic version roughly doubles Sharpe.
Regime-specific weights lift TSM Sharpe (0.559-0.734 vs 0.413-0.567), a tested way to change exposure by state.
Trailing stops rarely raise returns on a 71-instrument trend book, so the brake is a regime rule, not a stop.
EWMA vol needs horizon-specific scaling below sqrt(h) to size each future correctly.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: Trend pays in persistent moves and loses in sharp rebounds after panics; a vol-and-drawdown panic flag targets exactly the crash state without touching the trend signal itself.
blueprints.data_note: The portfolio-book harness has multi-asset trend 2008 onward; NT8 index futures, OANDA FX and gold, yields; a full 71-future set is not held.

evidence.bearing: FX-only trend is null and multi-asset trend is modest (about 0.3 OOS), so the brake must add to a weak base.
Vol-target sizing turned the TREND sleeve from Sharpe -0.16 to +0.16 (+0.32), so vol scaling is already worth keeping in this system.
The trend sleeve alone made Sharpe 0.26 inside the book, the baseline the brake must improve.

blueprints.risk: Panic states are rare (a handful since 2008), so the brake's gain may be impossible to tell from luck.
blueprints.first_test: On the portfolio-book trend sleeve 2008-2026, scale exposure to zero when the S&P is down over 12 months and its 1-month vol is in the top quintile; compare Sharpe and worst month against the vol-targeted sleeve, block bootstrap.
related: Carry-conditioned multi-asset trend with crash-state scaling
Multi-asset trend book with regime-dependent weights

blueprints.name: NQ hold hedge: puts vs VIX overlay vs smaller size
blueprints.idea: For a long NQ hold, compare three ways to cut drawdown at equal volatility: buy OTM puts, add a long-VIX overlay only above a VIX threshold, or simply hold less. The aim is to find whether any hedge beats a smaller position once the roll and premium costs are paid.
blueprints.market: NQ / SPX long hold

parts.why: Grade A: 5% OTM monthly puts earned 2.5% vs 5.8% for the S&P, and the same return came from just holding less equity, the core benchmark.
A static 10% OTM put overlay cut 2008 drawdown from -56.8% to -32.4% but cost 1.1%/yr; a dynamic rule cost 0.4%/yr.
A VIX overlay switched on only above a VIX threshold raised hedged-portfolio alpha in a theoretical test.
Long VIX futures lose about 30% a year to roll, the cost the theoretical VIX overlay ignores.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: All four parts price the same thing, the cost of crash insurance, and P120 sets the test the desk already uses: a hedge must beat simply holding less.
blueprints.data_note: NQ futures 2004 onward, VIX futures 2013 onward, Cboe index family (PUT benchmark used in portfolio-book-validate); no long S&P option price history beyond CME settlement IV (6 years).

evidence.bearing: The VIX stand-aside's drawdown cut was just less exposure, which is P120's finding on our data.
Inverse-variance sizing had the best drawdown of any arm (-26% vs -55%), the bar a hedge must beat.
A hedge can cut expected shortfall in a different book (FX trend), so a hedge test design exists here.

blueprints.risk: Without real option prices before 2020 the put arm rests on index proxies, and the VIX arm on futures only from 2013.
blueprints.first_test: NQ 2013-2026 at matched volatility: long VIX futures overlay when VIX is above 20 versus vol-target sizing alone; compare max drawdown and Sharpe, with the overlay charged its real roll.

also.name: Jump-model regime switch with dynamic tail cover
Index tail hedge chosen by trend state, not standing puts

blueprints.name: Stress-aware range bands for stops
blueprints.idea: Build stop and target bands from conformal range intervals whose calibration memory is weighted toward the current vol state, so bands widen properly in stress. The papers say recency-only calibration looks fine on average but under-covers in stress, exactly when stops get run.
blueprints.market: 34 desk instruments (FX, gold, indices)

parts.why: Recency-only conformal calibration is near nominal on average but under-covers in high-vol states for next-day high-low ranges.
Regime-switching AR/HAR forecasts of RV fit and forecast better out of sample, giving the state label for state-weighted calibration.
Leverage and semivariance terms carry the post-fall vol rise into the band centre.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: Coverage fails in stress because the calibration window is mostly calm days; conditioning the calibration on a vol state fixes the same flaw the desk's persistence fix targets.
blueprints.data_note: M1 bid/ask 2016-2026 for 34 instruments, the shipped point-in-time lines and sigma.

evidence.bearing: A regime nudge already cut the calm-vs-busy p75 miss from 5.6pp to 1.8pp, so much of this gap is already closed.
HAR-800 cut the 30-cell regime miss from 2.86pp to 1.41pp; the remaining miss is the target.
Stops are hit far more often right after bursts, where stress-state under-coverage would bite.

blueprints.risk: The desk's persistence and HAR-800 fixes may leave too little stress-state miss for a new method to matter.
blueprints.first_test: On the shipped 2023-2026 lines, compare p75/p90 coverage in the top vol-state quintile for state-weighted conformal versus current lines; pass if the stress-state miss falls by at least 1pp with no loss in calm states.

blueprints.name: VXN-extreme intraday band reversion on NQ
blueprints.idea: Fade NQ moves beyond an IV band (prior close plus or minus VXN/16) with a 30-minute exit, but only when VXN is at an extreme (below 20 or 30 and above), where the paper finds positive Sharpe; stand aside in the mid range.
blueprints.market: NQ futures

parts.why: Moves beyond the VXN/16 band revert intraday 85.2% of the time; the 30-minute exit has positive Sharpe only at VXN extremes (0.38 below 20, 0.64 at 30+).
Rough volatility (H about 0.1) means short-lag vol is very noisy, a reason the band and its vol regime should be read from IV, not short RV.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: The band is the move priced by implied vol for one day; extremes of VXN mark days when that pricing is most likely off. The fit is plausible but rests on one B-grade paper with unclear OOS.
blueprints.data_note: NT8 NQ minute data, VXN daily from the Cboe family.

evidence.bearing: Realised Nasdaq moves run about 0.84 of the VXN-priced move, so a VXN/16 band is crossed less often than a fair band and reversion looks high by construction.
Range passes but fading on calm-front days lost -0.05/-0.07R in both halves and on both instruments.
Fades lost net of spread in every ATR regime; the new angle is the IV-level extreme as the switch and a fixed 30-minute exit.
Daily vol-band fades on FX and gold showed no reversion, a caution on any band-fade.

blueprints.risk: The 85% 'reversion' rate may be a geometry artefact, as the desk's level-touch work has repeatedly shown, and costs at 30-minute holds may eat a small edge.
blueprints.first_test: NQ 2016-2026 with real tick costs: fade first band breaks at VXN extremes, 30-minute exit, versus the same entry at a band drawn at a random multiple of VXN (placebo band), by half.

blueprints.name: Calm-regime dealer gamma for overnight-hold sizing
blueprints.idea: In calm-VIX regimes only, use residual dealer gamma to forecast the size of the overnight gap, and size the NQ/ES overnight hold down when gamma points to a large gap. In stressed regimes ignore gamma and use IV alone.
blueprints.market: NQ and ES overnight hold

parts.why: Against HAR plus credit, SPX dealer gamma forecasts the overnight gap size out of sample only in low-VIX regimes (CW +5.82), not in stress.
Lower net gamma raises next-day effective spreads by about 9% per SD, a liquidity channel for why gamma would matter more in calm markets.
A pre-registered null on strike-local GEX walls, so only the aggregate gamma level is used, not walls.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: Dealer hedging flow matters most when other flow is thin, which is the calm regime; using it only for gap size keeps it out of direction, where the desk's gamma tests fail.
blueprints.data_note: OI/GEX nightly (CME OI by strike 2020-2026, Databento ES options 2020-2026), NT8 NQ/ES minute data for the gap; no SPX-option GEX.

evidence.bearing: In calm-VIX ES sessions short gamma added nothing beyond IV to next-session range, close to a direct refusal of P079.
The NQ calm-regime version is underpowered; the new angle is the overnight gap alone rather than the full session range.
The NQ overnight hold itself is unproven, so this only shapes risk on an uncertain base.
Short gamma days run wider on ES, so the gamma-size link exists at the session level.

blueprints.risk: The calm-regime ES null suggests IV already carries what gamma adds, and the overnight-gap sample is only about 6 years.
blueprints.first_test: ES and NQ 2020-2026, calm-VIX nights only: does residual GEX improve the forecast of |overnight gap| beyond VIX9D/VIX and HAR (Clark-West, block bootstrap), against a shifted-GEX placebo?

corroborations.title: Simple linear vol models are hard to beat
corroborations.finding: HAR-RV beats ARFIMA and AR (P717), beats NHITS, TFT, LSTM and GARCH on 80 S&P 100 stocks (P777), beats a COT-augmented random forest on weekly gold (R2 0.313 vs 0.125, P732); linear models beat Transformers on long-horizon forecasting (P285); and plain EWMA explains 40-45% of future RV variance across 47 futures, comparable to ARCH (P719). The desk's forecast-pick and vol-layer work (small gains from extra HAR terms) agree.
corroborations.markets: equity indices, single stocks, gold, multi-asset futures, FX

corroborations.title: Implied vol adds to realised-vol forecasts
corroborations.finding: Adding VIX to a lagged-RV forecast cuts S&P RMSE 9.15% (P781); an options-implied rough-Heston spot vol improves log-HAR at horizons up to a month (P667); reviews of 71 IV indices find IV carries information beyond RV (P808, P682); an IV-surface CNN factor helps on SSE 50 (P778). The desk's iv-forecast (7/7 instruments) and combined-range results confirm this on our data.
corroborations.markets: S&P 500, Chinese ETF options, global IV indices; desk: FX, gold, indices

corroborations.title: Long VIX futures bleed; the premium sits at the front
corroborations.finding: Rolled one-month VIX futures lost about 30% a year (P694); single VIX ETNs erode while long-medium/short-front combinations earn Sharpe 1.19-1.31 (P709); shorting in contango compounds strongly (P696); the basis forecasts futures, not VIX (P509); the variance premium is negative and term-structured (P132) and concentrated at short maturities (P342). The desk's vix-ratio-vx-futures and short-vx-rule show the same roll on our data.
corroborations.markets: VIX futures and ETNs, S&P variance swaps

corroborations.title: Equity returns cluster around scheduled Fed events
corroborations.finding: 49bp in the 24 hours before FOMC (P319); announcement days carry 55% of the equity premium (P133); all S&P excess return in even FOMC-cycle weeks (P714, P348, two versions of one study); FOMC-day pricing sits in the press-conference window (P757); and IV rises into FOMC (P318). P714 and P348 are the same authors' work, so they count as one source.
corroborations.markets: S&P 500 / US equities

corroborations.title: Regime switches cut drawdown more reliably than they add return
corroborations.finding: A jump-model switch raises S&P Calmar from 0.16 to 0.28-0.39 (P225); HMM expected-Sharpe sizing scores well OOS (P224); a sticky-regime HMM overlay cuts sector-book drawdown to 14.22% (P878); a 200-day SMA switch and a dynamic hedge both cut drawdown at lower cost than static puts (P540, P742). On our data the drawdown gains from stress filters vanish once vol-matched (stress-filter-hold-flat), so the papers' drawdown claims need that check.
corroborations.markets: S&P 500, DAX, multi-asset futures, sector ETFs

corroborations.title: Volatility is rough at short lags
corroborations.finding: Log-vol behaves like fractional Brownian motion with Hurst about 0.1 on many indices (P232), even rougher on range-based proxies (P858), and a multivariate fBm forecasts RV better than HAR (P660). The forecasting gain over HAR is claimed but not quantified in the pack.
corroborations.markets: global equity indices, multi-asset

contradictions.title: Does vol-managing add return, or only cut exposure?
contradictions.finding: P720 reports large alphas from scaling factor returns by inverse prior variance (market alpha 4.86% a year). P120 (grade A) finds that 5% OTM puts give the same return as just holding less equity, so the 'protection' was only lower exposure.
contradictions.settle: Compare each de-risking rule to buy-and-hold scaled to the same volatility, out of sample, net of costs, in both halves.
contradictions.our_evidence: vol-managed-mm underpowered (Sharpe 0.622 vs 0.628, worked 2004-14 then reversed) and stress-filter-hold-flat underpowered (drawdown cut was just less exposure): the desk sides with P120.

contradictions.title: Long memory (HAR) vs rough vol vs ML
contradictions.finding: HAR treats persistence as long memory; P232 says that is an artefact of rough vol (H about 0.1) and P660 says an fBm model beats HAR. P780 has signature features beating HAR intraday, while P777 has neural nets losing to HAR on every metric.
contradictions.settle: One walk-forward QLIKE horse race on the desk's 34 instruments with the same RV proxy, HAR versus a rough-vol forecast versus a signature model, with Diebold-Mariano tests.
contradictions.our_evidence: forecast-pick validated (persistence and HAR-800 near equal) and vol-layer-state-confirm-nudge context (extra HAR terms add 0.16%): leans toward simple models, no rough-vol test banked.

contradictions.title: Statistical loss vs economic value of a vol forecast
contradictions.finding: P779 says fit HAR under QLIKE to match the evaluation loss; P082 argues the loss-minimising forecast is not the one that gives the most value to a vol-timing investor (its low-frequency HAR-L wins on utility).
contradictions.settle: Score candidate forecasts both by QLIKE and by the Sharpe and worst month of the same vol-targeted book.
contradictions.our_evidence: vol-target validated: any sigma steadies risk and which sigma is used barely changes Sharpe (HAR vs live +0.00), so statistical gains did not become economic gains in sizing; they paid on the range lines instead.

contradictions.title: Jump model vs HMM for regime detection
contradictions.finding: P225 finds the jump model beats an HMM benchmark OOS on S&P (Sharpe 0.68-0.71 vs 0.51-0.55). P224 reports strong OOS Sharpes (0.86-3.00) from a three-state HMM expected-Sharpe signal on futures over a short 2016-2019 window.
contradictions.settle: Run both on the same NQ/ES daily data 2004-2026, same delay and costs, against vol-matched buy-and-hold.
contradictions.our_evidence: gr-hmm-trend-direction null (HMM trend gives no next-day FX direction) and regime-picks-rule-hmm underpowered: the HMM is a variance read here; no jump-model test banked.

contradictions.title: Long VIX as a hedge vs short VIX as carry
contradictions.finding: P698 says holding VIX above a threshold improves a hedged portfolio, and P561 goes long after high VIX; P694 shows rolled long VIX futures lose about 30% a year, and P696 makes money on the short side of the same contango.
contradictions.settle: Test the threshold-long-VIX overlay on tradable VX futures with real roll, against vol-target sizing at equal volatility.
contradictions.our_evidence: vix-ratio-vx-futures validated (VIX gives back after extremes, about 60% capturable on futures) and short-vx-rule underpowered: the desk leans toward the short side.

contradictions.title: Does dealer gamma matter in calm markets?
contradictions.finding: P079 finds residual SPX gamma forecasts overnight gap size only in calm regimes, highly significant. P774, a pre-registered test, finds GEX walls have no strike-local effect at all.
contradictions.settle: A calm-regime test of aggregate gamma on overnight gap size, beyond IV, with a shifted-GEX placebo, on ES and NQ.
contradictions.our_evidence: gex-range-iv-calm-es null and gex-range-iv-calm-nq underpowered for session range; wall-placebo null for walls: the desk sides against strike-local walls and has not tested the overnight gap.

themes.label: Trend, factors & portfolio
themes.summary: The strongest material in this pack is slow, multi-asset trend (time-series momentum on futures) plus the sizing layer around it: vol scaling, regime weights and diversification breadth. Our own book already agrees on the shape: trend on FX alone is null, broad multi-asset trend is modest (~0.3), and vol-target sizing is validated. The best new systems therefore add an untested regime or timing layer to a trend or index-beta core, not a new direction signal. Intraday momentum/breakout, FX factor premia and pairs/mean-reversion papers are mostly contradicted by stricter papers and by our own nulls, so they rank low.

blueprints.name: Multi-asset trend book with regime-dependent weights
blueprints.idea: Run 12-month time-series momentum across every market we hold (indices, gold, FX majors, rates proxies), each sized to the same vol. Then tilt the weight on trend up or down by a two-state market regime, as P768 does, instead of a fixed weight. No stops on the trend legs.
blueprints.market: Multi-asset: index CFDs/futures (NQ, ES, SPX500, GER40), gold, FX majors

parts.why: 12-month own-return predicts next month across 58 futures; the core signal.
Risk-scaled futures momentum with Sharpe above 1.2 at daily/weekly/monthly holding confirms the vol-scaled version.
Two-state regime weights lifted OOS Sharpe by 0.15-0.23 over fixed momentum; the layer our book never tried.
Breadth not convexity drives trend Sharpe (single market 0.17 vs 73-market portfolio 0.72), so the book must stay wide.
No stop configuration improved a trend/ARP book net of costs, so exits stay signal-driven.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: All parts describe the same slow futures trend premium at the same monthly horizon; P768 and P769 change how much of it you hold, not which way you trade.
blueprints.data_note: OANDA M1/daily FX, gold and index CFDs 2016-2026 plus NT8 ES/NQ/YM/RTY; ^TNX from 1970 and US curve for a rates leg; the existing portfolio-book harness.

evidence.bearing: FX-only trend is dead and broad multi-asset was ~0.3 OOS, so the book must be multi-asset and the regime layer must add on top of ~0.3.
Forecast-sigma sizing turned the TREND sleeve from -0.16 to +0.16 Sharpe, so vol scaling is the base, not the test.
Trend is already a sleeve in a book with net Sharpe 1.06 but deflated 0.49; the regime tilt must beat this sleeve, not zero.
Scaling trend exposure by COT crowding state added nothing, so the regime input should be market state (P768), not positioning.

blueprints.risk: With ~10 years of CFD data the regime tilt's gain (0.15-0.23 Sharpe in P768) is near or below what we can detect.
blueprints.first_test: On the existing trend sleeve, compare P768-style two-state regime weights (fitted on earlier years only) against the fixed-weight vol-targeted sleeve; benchmark = current trend sleeve Sharpe, bar = CI clear of zero on the difference.
related: Carry-conditioned multi-asset trend with crash-state scaling
Multi-asset trend with a panic-state brake

blueprints.name: Index beta switched by a jump-model regime, vol-managed
blueprints.idea: Hold the equity index long only while a two-state statistical jump model says the market is in its calm state; otherwise sit in cash. Size the held position by inverse recent variance. Cross-check the switch with an HMM expected-Sharpe signal.
blueprints.market: SPX500, NAS100, GER40 (index CFDs) and ES/NQ futures

parts.why: Grade A: jump-model switch beat buy-and-hold net of costs on S&P, DAX and Nikkei (S&P Sharpe 0.48 to 0.68-0.71) with 1-10 day delays.
Grade A: HMM expected-Sharpe signal on 15 futures, OOS with costs; a second regime read on the same daily features.
Scaling by prior variance gave market alpha 4.86% a year; sizes the time spent in the market.
Momentum crashes cluster after market falls in high-vol states; supports leaving the index when the jump model flips.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: All three describe one effect: equity returns per unit of risk are poor in persistent high-vol states, so stepping aside and scaling down in them improves risk-adjusted return.
blueprints.data_note: Index CFD daily/M1 2016-2026, NT8 futures, SPY 1-min; VIX from 1990 for a longer daily check.

evidence.bearing: A VIX-stress half-size rule added nothing beyond vol targeting, so the jump model must beat vol-target alone, not buy-and-hold.
Moreira-Muir on NQ gave no Sharpe gain but the best drawdown; the jump switch must add to that.
HMM next-day direction on FX was null; this tests a persistent index on/off state with multi-week holds, which that null did not.
HMM vol states picking intraday tactics was underpowered; different use (exposure on/off).

blueprints.risk: Our nulls say vol-target already captures most of what a regime switch adds; the jump penalty may only cut drawdown, not raise Sharpe.
blueprints.first_test: Walk-forward P225 jump model (refit yearly, 1-day delay) on SPX500/NAS100 daily, scored as vol-target-plus-switch minus vol-target alone on net Sharpe and max drawdown; benchmark = vol-target arm from vol-managed-mm.

blueprints.name: FOMC-cycle timing on the index beta sleeve
blueprints.idea: Hold the index beta sleeve with full weight in even weeks of the FOMC cycle and on scheduled announcement days, and reduced weight in odd weeks. This is a calendar timing layer on top of an existing long book.
blueprints.market: SPX500, NAS100, ES/NQ

parts.why: Even FOMC-cycle weeks earn +12bp/day over odd weeks, 1994-2016, significant at 1%.
Earlier sample 1994-2013: excess return earned in weeks 0, 2, 4, 6 (+13.6 / +10.1 bp).
Announcement days earn 3.36%/yr of the 6.19% equity premium; a second calendar slice of the same mechanism.
Vol-scales the held exposure so calendar days do not get dominated by high-vol weeks.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: P714/P348/P133 all say the equity premium is paid around Fed and macro information events; it is a timing tilt on beta, not a new signal.
blueprints.data_note: FOMC dates (fomc-range-share used 84 meetings), calendar store, index CFD and futures daily, VIX from 1990 for a long pre-2016 check.

evidence.bearing: Our one surviving direction base rate is an FOMC-cycle effect in FX, which makes an FOMC-cycle equity effect plausible on our data.
FOMC days carry more variance in fixed windows; sizing must account for it.
The core-beta sleeve exists already, so this is an overlay test on a live sleeve.

blueprints.risk: The effect was published in 2013-2019 and may have decayed post-publication, as P042 found for FX factors.
blueprints.first_test: On SPX500 daily 2016-2026 (and SPX index since 1994 for replication), mean even-week minus odd-week return with a block bootstrap and a placebo of shifted cycle dates; benchmark = shifted-calendar placebo distribution.

blueprints.name: Gold trend gated by joint gold-bond momentum
blueprints.idea: Hold gold long only when both gold and Treasuries have positive 12-month momentum, otherwise cash, sized to constant vol. A gold-specific version of time-series momentum.
blueprints.market: XAUUSD (gold CFD), with US 10y yields / bond proxy

parts.why: Joint gold+bond 12m momentum state lifts GLD Sharpe to 0.59 (0.81 with cash) with lower drawdown.
Gold is one of the 58 futures where 12-month own momentum predicts next month.
Risk-scaled momentum sizing; keeps gold's risk steady across regimes.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: Gold behaves as a rates asset part of the time; requiring bond momentum to agree picks the times both legs of that driver point the same way.
blueprints.data_note: Gold M1/daily 2016-2026 OANDA; ^TNX/^FVX from 1970 and US curve from FRED for the bond leg; longer gold daily from Yahoo/FRED for a pre-2016 check.

evidence.bearing: Gold is driven by rates in only ~19% of windows, which may explain when the joint filter helps or not.
VIX-spike gold bids are null, so the regime input should be bonds, not fear.
Macro quadrant tilts on gold were underpowered; monthly samples are small here too.
A 1/3/12-month trend blend on gold at 1-5 day horizons was underpowered; this test is at the monthly horizon the paper used.

blueprints.risk: Monthly sampling gives few independent states in 10 years of CFD data, so it will likely be underpowered without a long pre-2016 gold history.
blueprints.first_test: Replicate P753 on monthly gold and 10y-yield momentum 1975-2026 (data permitting), then score 2016-2026 OOS; benchmark = gold 12m TSMOM alone and buy-and-hold gold.

blueprints.name: FX carry + momentum gated by global FX vol, on a wider currency set
blueprints.idea: Rank currencies on carry and momentum, but go flat or cut size when global FX volatility innovations spike. Widen the set to the 19 Yahoo crosses including EM to fix the power problem in our earlier 8-currency tests.
blueprints.market: G10 + EM FX (Yahoo daily 19 crosses, OANDA majors)

parts.why: Optimal currency portfolios using carry and momentum add ~0.5 Sharpe and reduce crash risk; real rates and current account do not help.
Currency momentum over 48 currencies, up to 10% a year, costs considered.
High-yield currencies fall when global FX vol spikes; the vol-innovation gate.
Unlevered carry Sharpe ~0.5 with skew -1.2; leverage amplifies crash risk, so size small and capped.
Short-dollar carry earns most in bad times; warns the gate may cut the best months.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: Carry is paid for crash risk tied to global FX vol (P036, P040); momentum diversifies it (P044). A vol gate attacks the known crash channel.
blueprints.data_note: Yahoo daily 19 crosses incl. EM (dormant), OECD short rates (EUR dead since 2026-02), CME FX IV 6 years; no OIS or live non-US short rates.

evidence.bearing: 8-currency carry rank-IC +0.079 [-0.030, +0.192]: right sign, too few currencies; the wider set is the new angle.
8-currency momentum was negative; P042 also found post-publication decay.
Already tried a risk-off gate on carry; MDE ~+1.4 Sharpe, so the gate itself is untested at real power.
Rate-differential momentum Sharpe 0.13 1976-2026; carry level, not its change, is the signal here.

blueprints.risk: P042 shows FX factor Sharpe fell from +0.39 to -0.32 after publication, so even a well-powered test may find nothing.
blueprints.first_test: On 19 currencies monthly 2005-2026, carry+momentum equal-risk book with and without a P036 FX-vol-innovation gate; benchmark = ungated book, judged on net Sharpe and worst-month loss.
related: Slow G10 blend: Taylor value + carry + momentum

blueprints.name: NQ noise-band momentum timed by first-half-hour volatility
blueprints.idea: Trade the validated noise-band breakout on NQ/SPY, but only (or with larger size) on days when the first 30 minutes were in the high-vol tercile, where P725 finds intraday momentum is strongest.
blueprints.market: NQ futures, SPY 1-min, ES

parts.why: Noise-area breakout on SPY 1-min, Sharpe 1.33 vol-targeted; reproduced on our SPY data.
First 30-min return predicts the last half hour; R2 3.3% in the high first-half-hour vol tercile vs 0.6% low.
Across 60+ futures the rest-of-day return predicts the last 30 minutes, attributed to hedging demand; the flow behind the effect.
Grade A falsification on MNQ: 14 OHLCV families fail OOS after friction; the bar any variant must clear.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: P006, P725 and P716 all describe late-day continuation of an early move, driven by hedging flows that are larger on high-vol mornings.
blueprints.data_note: NT8 ES/NQ minute data, SPY 1-min IBKR 2007-2024, NAS100 OANDA bid/ask M1.

evidence.bearing: NQ passed every part (net Sharpe 1.23), ES missed; the base rule is alive on NQ.
The rule reproduces on SPY in-sample.
Tuning band/VIX/NR4 filters did not beat the paper rule; a first-30-min realised-vol tercile was not in that design space.
The first-half-hour to last-half-hour trade alone fails net; this uses it as a filter, not a trade.
Spreading the rule over 21 markets lost money; keep it to NQ/SPY.

blueprints.risk: Adding a filter to a rule already near its noise floor risks overfitting; P871 says most intraday OHLCV edges die net of costs.
blueprints.first_test: On NQ futures 2016-2026, noise-band daily P&L split by first-30-min realised-vol tercile (known at 10:00 ET), net of 1 tick + $4.50; benchmark = unfiltered rule and shuffled-tercile placebo.

also.name: Gamma-gated noise-band momentum

blueprints.name: Risk budgeting across desk sleeves by HRP vs equal risk
blueprints.idea: Keep the existing sleeves (core beta, trend, carry, FOMC drift, Rule A) but replace fixed equal-risk weights with hierarchical risk parity or a collision-aware cap, judged on drawdown, not Sharpe.
blueprints.market: Desk portfolio book (multi-asset CFDs)

parts.why: HRP beat ERC and MVO on Sharpe (1.02 vs 0.94 vs 0.71) with lower concentration, synthetic universe.
HRP out-of-sample vol 0.067 vs 0.093 IVP vs 0.116 CLA in simulation.
Penalising crowded common trades cut max drawdown 23.6% to 14.1% at the same Sharpe.
Inverse-variance often matches ERC; sets the simple benchmark.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: All are allocation layers on given return streams; they cannot add edge, only cut drawdown and concentration, which is what the prop-firm use of the book needs.
blueprints.data_note: Portfolio-book harness sleeve returns 2008-2026 and Rule A daily book 2020-2026.

evidence.bearing: Equal-risk book net Sharpe 1.06, deflated 0.49, max DD 17.5%: the benchmark to beat on drawdown.
Correlation-cluster ERC on Rule A could not beat 1R per trade on Sharpe; target drawdown instead.
Rule A is uncorrelated with the book, so it belongs as a separate cluster in HRP.
Prop daily-loss limits end most 2x attempts, so drawdown is the metric that matters.

blueprints.risk: P788 shows individually significant Sharpes cannot be ranked against each other, so any Sharpe gain will be noise; only a drawdown gain is plausible.
blueprints.first_test: Walk-forward HRP and inverse-variance vs fixed equal-risk on the sleeve returns 2008-2026, primary metric max drawdown and worst-5% day; benchmark = current equal-risk book.

blueprints.name: Index tail hedge chosen by trend state, not standing puts
blueprints.idea: Instead of standing OTM puts, hedge the index beta sleeve only when the trend/regime switch is off, using a dynamic hedge or a VIX-long overlay when VIX is high.
blueprints.market: SPX500/NAS100 beta with VIX futures or index short

parts.why: Grade A: standing 5% OTM puts cut return from 5.8% to 2.5% a year, the same as holding less equity.
Dynamic hedge drags 0.4%/yr vs 1.1% for static puts with similar crisis protection.
Holding VIX when VIX is high gave CAPM alpha 0.75 (t=16) in theory, no costs.
Jump-model state decides when the hedge is on.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: Static insurance is overpriced (VRP), so the hedge should only be held in the states where crashes cluster; the regime switch supplies those states.
blueprints.data_note: VIX family from 1990 and VX settles 2013-; index CFDs; no SPX option chain history beyond CME settlement IV.

evidence.bearing: Short-VX rule underpowered; VIX futures roll costs make P698's theoretical VIX overlay hard to hold.
VIX inversion predicts wider weeks (range), a usable on-switch for the hedge.
A VIX stress half-size rule added nothing beyond vol-target, a warning that state-hedging may duplicate vol targeting.

blueprints.risk: Vol targeting already cuts exposure in the same states, so the hedge may add cost without extra protection.
blueprints.first_test: On SPX500 2008-2026, vol-target sleeve plus a short-index hedge switched on by the jump-model state vs vol-target alone, judged on max drawdown per unit of return lost; benchmark = P120's 'hold less equity' arm.

blueprints.name: NQ IV-band reversion only at VXN extremes
blueprints.idea: Fade NQ moves beyond the implied-vol band around the prior close, but only when VXN is at its extremes, where P850 found the exit Sharpe positive.
blueprints.market: NQ futures / NAS100

parts.why: 85.2% of NQ moves past the IV band revert (n=860); Sharpe positive only at VXN extremes (0.38/0.64).
Grade A: 14 MNQ intraday families fail after friction; the cost bar.
Grade A: 0/225 ORB cells survive $25/RT; gross edges vanish net.

blueprints.mechanism_fit: Reversion after a band touch is a liquidity-provision trade; vol extremes are when compensation for providing it is largest.
blueprints.data_note: NT8 NQ minute data, VXN from Cboe family, CME settlement IV.

evidence.bearing: Extension fades were positive gross but 3-8x under cost: the same failure mode.
Fade/follow by NQ gamma regime failed; the VXN gate is a different regime input.
IV regime did not pick losing fade/follow days on FX; not tested on NQ IV bands.

blueprints.risk: Hit rate is high but payoff per trade is small, so costs very likely eat it, as in every similar desk test.
blueprints.first_test: On NQ futures 2016-2026, band-touch fade with 30-min exit in VXN top/bottom decile vs middle, net of 1 tick + $4.50; benchmark = same rule on random times with matched VXN.
